Title: 6 reasons to join the circus
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content: Reason 1: learn cool physical skills There are so many things to do in the circus. Handstands! Fire spinning! Juggling! Fire juggling! Trapeze! Silks! Contortion! At some point, my favorite Wikipedia page was this: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_circus_skills. I love learning random skills, and in the circus, there’s always another skill to learn. I learned to juggle three balls over COVID Quarantine, and throughout high school, I would flex my juggling skills by juggling the tennis balls at tennis games rather than hitting them (by doing so I lost many games⁠01 ). Then, in my senior year, I learned that there was more to juggling than three balls. Indeed, beyond three, there exist numbers like 4, 5, even 6, and *gasp* 7?!? And a few more numbers above that, probably, though I haven’t discovered them yet. Suddenly, a whole new world of possibilities opened up to me. Since then, I’ve been obsessed—there’s always something new, something to break up the routine. If this whole MIT thing doesn’t work out, I know where I’m going next. Reason 2: Artificial Intelligence can’t replace you I’ve recently for some reason watched a bunch of AI gymnastics videos on YouTube. And gosh, they’re terrible. Why did his head twist 360 degrees in that front handspring? Why does she have four legs and six knees now? And—oh, she just disappeared into thin air. sheer cosmic horror… (credit: https://www.creativebloq.com/ai/ai-art/ai-gymnastics-videos-are-captivatingly-horrific) It’s comforting in a way, knowing that AI companies can claim to have solved the Navier-Stokes, yet something so seemingly intuitive as understanding how human bodies move is so foreign to AI. It’s also comforting to know that AI still can’t do what I…still can’t do either. But I’m working on it, I promise! The MIT Gymnastics Club offers beginner gymnastics classes every Tuesday, and I’ve been going on and off since last year (with long periods of “off”, depending on my psets :( ). I’m still scared to try any acrobatics moves that involve my head upside down in midair, so I’ve been working on handstands! Nowadays, I’m addicted to handstands—I also keep seeing videos online of one armed handstands and handstand pushups. They look so cool! I want to do that someday. I’ve been practicing in my room in between psets, to get the blood rushing back to my brain after my quantum mechanics problems drains it all. In my room, I have an air mattress still inflated from three weeks ago, I hosted someone for Math Prize for Girls ⁠02 . I never bothered to deflate and put it away because I’m lazy :P and it’s fun to lie on and most importantly, it serves as a nice crash pad for when I do handstands away from the wall. my crash pad! Reason 3: Shorten your nerve endings Life is too short. Your nerve endings are not short enough… There’s a circus center in Somerville, and a week ago, I convinced my friend Grace L. ‘30 to sign up for an Aerial Ropes class there! Aerial Rope, also known as corde lisse, is a smooth rope that people climb up and do cool flowy moves on. 03 It was a lot more…painful than I expected. Watching circus acts in videos really does not do justice to how painful things are—there’s a lot of pressure on sensitive parts of the body, like armpits or the back of knees, and lots of unnatural poses. Here are some quotes from during the class: “doom and despair” “circus is like self inflicted torture” “help i’m dying” “AHHH” Now match the quotes to the pictures: okay i look kind of happy here grace says i look like i'm having a great nap ahhhhhh wheeee Previous Next Having experienced it for myself, it’s a lot more impressive to me now, that professional circus artists can do everything so gracefully. The instructor for our class reassured us that after a while, our nerve endings would get shorter (hmm is this reassuring? I’m not sure…) and we’d be able to feel less of it. Reason 4: juggling classes? juggling balls I cannot express the disappointment that I felt that day, when I was just a wee high schooler reading MIT blogs, when I searched up “juggling” in MIT Blogs, got SO excited when over a hundred results popped up, and then realized that most of the entries were about juggling classes, UROPs, and schedules. Then, I thought I had been clickbaited. Alas, now I realize that such is the reality of MIT. I haven’t properly juggled in two months, and I haven’t learned a single new juggling trick in the past year. As a prefrosh, I would have found this repulsive. What?!? No juggling? Had I lost all mischief in my life? But with upcoming pset deadlines, scary midterms⁠04 , UROP meetings, I feel as if every moment I have must be spent doing something productive that contributes to My Future Career—scrambling for internships, obtaining a good GPA—and there is simply no time to pause and throw a couple of balls into the air. But perhaps there’s a simple solution—switch My Future Career to the circus… (i juggled fire last year :) it was so scary) Reason 4: having an odd number of wheels in your life This year, I doubled the number of wheels that I commute to class with from a unicycle to a duocycle dicycle tandem unicycle bicycle! And it’s so much more efficient. I’ve gone to all my lectures this semester (barring being sick or having conflicting classes :P) ! I lost track of the amount of times I didn’t go to lecture last year because of how cold it was in the morning and how much I simply didn’t want to step out of my room. Or because of how sleepy I was. Actually, as I’m writing this, I realize that both of these reasons for not going to classes have not disappeared because I now own a bike but because it’s not winter yet, and all my classes start past noon. But my point is, it decreases the activation energy hump by so much. I love my bike :) Although more boring, a bike is a lot faster than a unicycle. Double the wheels, double the speed, I suppose. For a week or so last year, unicycling was my primary mode of transportation to my classes, but I soon realized that the speed of a unicycle is in that awkward zone where it’s slightly faster than walking pace, but only slightly—which meant that when I unicycled on the sidewalk⁠05 , passing people took long enough to be slightly awkward. And not to mention that my legs get tired very fast, so I had to pause every twenty seconds to give my thighs a rest. My unicycle sat in my room, and then in the Juggling Club storage closet for a long while before I decided to pick it up again to learn some new tricks two weeks ago. blurry me with my fancy unicycle gear (aka wrist protectors, shin guards, elbow pads, and knee pads. i don’t wanna break my bones ) I’ve been inspired by freestyle unicycling, a sport that I’ve never really heard about until two months ago. There are some videos online, and it’s really impressive how people can make riding the unicycle flow so well—it’s almost like ice skating. I can’t say the same about my own unicycling skills: for the life of me, I just can’t figure out how to turn right.⁠06 I can turn left with no problem, but when I try leaning the other way? Nope! I’ve realized that it’s actually kind of relaxing⁠07 to spend two hours learning a new unicycling trick. In the days when I feel like I’m living problem set to problem set (every time I submit one, there’s always another…), it’s nice to spend time on something that is not for any class, any UROP, or any club, and purely for my own enjoyment. Having hobbies is great :) and I wish I had more time for them… Also, because I now no longer go anywhere without my bike, I also carry my unicycle on my bike. It’s very cursed, but decently stable (only slightly wobbly side to side when I turn sharply). Now it’s a tricycle, I guess? sometimes i get funny glances when biking down Dorm Row like this. i feel like it must look like a unicorn or something, with an extra wheel sticking out the front like this But someone else has me beat… on my way to unicycle, I passed by this monster of a “bike”. what the heck. It has like 5 wheels. and a xylophone… Previous Next Reason 6: no midterms or psets Yeah, I’m a bit burnt out. Could you tell? Perhaps now you’ve seen through the façade, and now realize that the secret second purpose of this blog is to complain about my psets and midterms. I think fall semester of sophomore year is the first semester I’ve felt genuinely overwhelmed about classwork. I’m taking five classes, and sometimes it feels like I’m doing nothing but rush from problem set to problem set, with no time in between to think about them. MIT can feel like a bubble sometimes. Sometimes, I feel like I can float forever in that bubble, in a familiar routine, watching the weeks pass by—assignment after assignment, test after test, commitment after commitment. Yet, at other times, that bubble seems to trap me—an endless cycle of routine, motivated by stress—and I think to myself, “why am I doing this?” Is it really worth it, rushing headlong into a career in academia or industry or whatever scientific thing my eventual degree in physics and/or mathematics this leads to? Because suppose I really did want to join the circus. Maybe I’ve joked about it so much that it has grown on me, and maybe this is just burnt-out me talking, and maybe it’s a stupid and unfounded dream—and sometimes it sounds like that, in this world where it seems like everyone is looking for the next quant internship or UROP opportunity—but I’ve been thinking…if I continue in this race, in the future, if I have a stable job⁠08 will I regret not pursuing my imagination and my whimsy? But will I have the courage to step off the path that seems like what everyone expects for me, to step back willingly from the cycle of stress and maximizing productivity? We’ll see…

Title: apple picking in october
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: every fall, sometime in october, a horde of mit students travel in a bunch of long yellow cars to an orchard an hour west of campus. like sleepy ants we straggle out of our buses and crawl over the apple-laden hills; as the sun starts to descend towards the horizon, and winds shake flame-red leaves on limber branches, we make our journey back home. that is to say – apple picking! yippee! apple picking is a yearly activity sponsored by dormcon,⁠01 mit’s student government body for everyone who lives in dorms. they host biweekly meetings where they discuss dorm policy, as well as interfacing with mit admin to advocate for student quality of life in the dorms. they also sponsor fun activities! this year, apple picking was a source of some consternation for my dorm, east campus. we’re one of the bigger dorms on campus, with around 400 people, but we received what some people felt was an unfairly low number of spots to go apple picking – indeed, we only had space for about half of the people who were interested. forms went around asking people what the maximum amount they would be willing to pay to go apple picking was. in the end, it stayed free, but a lottery and a five-dollar commitment fee made it slightly higher stakes than it otherwise would’ve been. on friday, october 9th, i was emailed saying i’d been selected through lottery! yay. day of! i wake up super early.⁠02 i put on a sweater and meet other ec people and start heading westside; then we realize it’s pretty cold, so me and a few other people run back in to get more jacket⁠03 we go to maseeh⁠04 and wait. we turn in a liability waiver that says “i know if i fall off a tree and die it’s my fault”. i wave to various friends from various other dorms. i realize that in my rush to leave the dorm, i hadn’t brought any tangerines⁠05 to eat. i start to feel hungry. food time! first, i realize that my pocket still holds a couple pieces of pita bread yoinked from terrascope lunch the thursday before. yippee! unfortunately i do seek more, so i run over to concord market⁠06 and buy two things of yogurt. one of them is a yogurt drink that i fell in love with while staying the summer here in 2025. nowadays it’s a rare treat, but whatever! i deserve it. i run back and realize there was no need to run back, because the buses are not moving at all. some of the tetazoo seniors are also going to concord; eric and an, two tetazoo sophomores, go to dunkin. i wait in line and talk to jsin. finally we get in the bus and start moving! the buses are sorted by dorm, so i sit next to jsin from florey and try my best to sleep. i’m…not sure how successful that was? like it’s a yellow school bus, so it’s quite uncomfortable and bouncy, but you know i try my best. i get some nice pictures of fall foliage too okay in hindsight this picture is bad for showing the pretty colors growing up in southern california we don’t really get these reds and oranges and yellows – i’m sure it’s obnoxious every time i point it out to the easterners around me. we finally arrive at the orchard! it’s really pretty. we all pour out of our various buses and scramble to enter the orchard. i get a bit confused about who i’m going in with, but eventually i find a group of five: me, jsin, serena also from ec, charles burton-connor, and freddy french house. after receiving our maybe ~4 gallon bag, we enter the orchard! how this orchard is set up is basically there are like 20 different varieties of apple trees, organized into neat little lines that sprawl over the ups and downs of the hills. unfortunately no one in my group was an apple connoisseur, so we kind of just wandered around tasting different apples and deciding which ones we liked. “oh these are nice!” “these are pretty sweet.” “i don’t like how mealy these ones are…” eventually if an apple met a certain (low) criteria of goodness, its fellows went into our bag. i was feeling kind of sleepy but i got woken up by the prospect of climbing things. i climbed lots of trees! very fun. there were also a bunch of very rickety, very scary ladders, but i mostly avoided them. look how happy! and so we wandered ‘round the undulating hills, collecting apples. every once in a while at mit, i find myself thinking of the end of the third lord of the rings book, where the newfound prosperity of the shire is described by something like pyramids of peach pits like stacks of conquered skulls, or something like that. apple picking did make me feel like that like wow look at all those apples cheese! Previous Next there’s some fun things at the orchard, like the apple blasters (where you get to shoot apples out of these huge air-powered cannons at targets) (sorry i forgot to get pictures) or this big windmill thing, or trucks pulling big carts with haybales that you can sit on.⁠07 eventually we ran out of things to do and made our way towards the exit. we bought some apple cider donuts⁠08 and then walked back to the bus, where they had two big boxes of apple cider donuts for free. so i ended up eating like 3 of them! yay. long bus ride back. i sleep (this time i have the window seat so that makes it easier). our bus gets back a bit later than the new house and bc buses, so me and jsin and selena have to rush to the stud to find freddy and charles. we pour out our wealth of red-and-green gold on a table. charles has some sort of interview (??), but we go around in a circle around and pick the ones we like. then i have to go to dance practice lol…⁠09 LOOK AT ALL THOSE APPLES overall fun time! i am glad to have frolicked outside among smiling friends. would do again :) pie time yay i go home, apple-laden.⁠10 what else is there to do but bake a pie? i’ve been doing a LOT of baking recently – it’s probably the main non-academic thing that i find myself doing over and over again. it’s just calming to do something with my hands and then have a tangible result that i can give to people that i care about. so with all of this raw material with me, obviously there is a thing to do! i kind of got outbuzzed on the pie thing because on the day of apple picking, george (a senior on my floor) hosted his event fallazoo, where he bakes a bunch of autumny desserts and puts on over the garden wall in the lounge. that day i was a little busy so all i could do was help peel and slice some apples before i had to go somewhere else. but later that day i was able to make some crust!⁠11 i’d never made pie crust before – usually i just buy the premade ones from the frozen section in the grocery store – but since tetazoo has communal flour and butter and sugar, i figured why not. i dug up a food processor from our appliances cabinet⁠12 and made two big balls of dough, which i then put in the fridge. the pie-making⁠13 itself would have to wait a bit, until monday night. that day i got hot pot with some friends; after we got back, i recruited one of them (yale, class of 30) to help me make the pie! i cooked up the sauce while he sliced the apples; after i rolled out the dough, we carefully ladled our apples into the pie, stacking them tall and high and then draping the other pie dough over it. the effect was somewhat like a gently-rounded ufo, or perhaps a lava dome. this went into the oven. approximately 20 minutes in someone came into glounge to tell me that the oven was filled with smoke. this is bad! it turns out that some of the pie juices had dripped onto the floor of the oven and were starting to burn; hua helped me clean it up. but at least the pie was gorgeous… look at how prettyy i held a brief eating party for this pie in tetazoo kitchen, complete with leftover coolwhip from fallazoo. the guests were: everyone in my apple picking group bunch of tetafrosh and tetafroshfriends in the kitchen freddy’s roommate will thank you will for looking enthused although this was a pretty good pie success, there were definitely some lessons i learned. first of all, the dough is significantly easier to roll out if you give it a bit more time to warm up after taking it out from the fridge; second of all, PUT A PAN UNDER THE PIE SO THAT THE JUICES DON’T LIGHT ON FIRE. these lessons i kept close to my heart as i prepared for the Second Pie. after all there are soooooo many apples left pie 1.5 – distracted by pumpkin pie in preparation for the 2nd apple pie, i made another batch of pie crust. unfortunately this pie crust was called into action by a birthday celebration, where we made audrey a pumpkin pie! so my apple pie plans got slightly delayed. okay there was supposed to be a picture here but i guess i forgot to take a picture :skull: apple pie 2: electric boogaloo i made yet another batch of pie crust to prepare for this pie. ngl this pie crust sat in the fridge for a while – i had a pretty busy week where i had to write 2 earth science tests for huso-india, had a 12.004 pset that was bothering me, and generally felt kind of overwhelmed. but after i got past that, and after i realized that the apples were starting to become elderly, i felt a new wind on my back pushing me towards making more pie. this time i felt somewhat inspired – i wanted to make a bunch of mini pies in a muffin tray. i would roll out little circles, fill them up with some apple, and then bake them. unfortunately it became REALLY annoying to roll out the pie crust into little circles so i gave up after three of them. but they also turned out really cute! (except for i forgot to eggwash them so they weren’t as pretty as they could’ve been) the other two were eaten before i took this picture yeah so i gave up on that idea. instead i remade another big pie! once again i rolled out the pie crust and stacked the apples nice and tall. even after cramming as many apples as i could in, i still had some left over… so i put them into the uncrusted muffin tray to make little apple crisps. i think i had to go somewhere after i put the pie in the oven (don’t exactly remember why ??) but my delightful floormates removed my adorable child at the perfect time. yay 2nd pie! this one is less golden brown but still delicious also shoutout to sage who made the crisp topping for the apple crisp using our communal oats. look at how nice it looks too they are browning fully baked! Previous Next and with that i was able to use up all of my apples i think! these various sweet treats went to a wide variety of people – the small pies were consumed by me, liam, and hua; the apple crisps by various tetazoans in the early morning hours. for this big pie, it, too, went to a multitude of friends – some for scarlet, kian, and charles from burton-connor; some for rukevwe from slugfest; and the rest for starving tetazoans seeking a piece of warm sun in the cold harsh reality of midterm season.

Title: bentry picnic
Author: Alejandro B. '30
Article Content: [important author’s note: this actually happened four weeks ago] [i’m sorry] ‘Twas was the night before the weekend. Two midterms later and many Uber Eats orders later I had made it through another week at MIT. How? I don’t know. It still feels like I just arrived on campus. I am unsure of when that feeling is going to unstick. One little trick I have used to enjoymaxx this semester is to not put too much stress over my grades! Us freshmen are on P/NR⁠01 and (checks grades) I am definitely making the most out of it. I also had many things to look forward to this weekend. Especially on Sunday which was when I had the long-awaited Bentry picnic. But but but…what is Bentry?? I’M GETTING TO THAT. I live in MacGregor House, located along the stretch of dorm row. It is far enough away to make me late to my morning classes (it’s the building’s fault; not mine), but close enough to uhhh…live I guess? I initially chose MacGregor largely because of the fact that 99% of the rooms are singles. I did not and still don’t believe in sacrificing my privacy for the traditional college experience. Another fact about MacGregor is that it is split into nine “entries” from A entry to J entry; i entry is imaginary. I am in B entry, aka Bentry, aka B stands for best, composed of the 10th, 11th, and 12th floor. I quickly met a lot of people from Bentry, largely in part because of the entry’s social nature. Also in part because of our weekly study breaks, planned by our entry chairs and GRA – shout out to Ryan, Jessie and Tobi. This week was especially exciting because for our study break we were going on a picnic to the Boston commons! Since arriving on campus, I had only been over to the other side of the Harvard bridge once; so this was an exciting opportunity to explore the big city. I spent all week brainstorming ~ what should I cook? ~ I wanted to have a dish that represented my culture which would also fit the theme of a picnic. Honestly, my indecisiveness got the better of me but eventually I landed on “tequeños.” If you know what tequeños are: I am glad, I am sure your life has been better since. If you do not know what tequeños are: In essence, they are a better type of cheese stick. In Venezuela, they are eaten everywhere and growing up I have probably had over 300 tequeños. I am a fatty. On Saturday at 7:00 PM, I set out to buy the ingredients. On Saturday at 7:20 PM I realized that this was not going to be feasible. To make tequeños I needed fresh white cheese for frying, usually from some type of hispanic brand. I had overlooked the fact that I was no longer in Kissimmee⁠02 and getting my hands on hispanic ingredients was more challenging than anticipated. After weighting my options with my cooking skills I decided that the best thing I could do for my culture was to buy the tequeños! Becoming a good cook will have to be left for another blog… And so, the day had arrived, we made our way to the Kendall/MIT train station. Two stops later we were at Park Street, which stops right on top of Boston Commons. I felt like I was transported to a 2010s feel good movie walking through beautiful trees in the middle of a city bustling with people. As per Susila’s recommendation we walked all the way down to the Public Garden, even going right through a walkathon occurring that same day. Once we found a spot we laid out our blankets, and everyone started setting up the food they had brought. So. Where were the tequeños? Going back, I actually placed an order for the tequeños as we were walking to Kendall station. I was mildly stressed while we walked because with each slow step taken the delivery time got closer and closer. Thankfully, we arrived right on time. Taking a short detour from the group, I got my delivery of 20 tequeños from a local Venezuelan place and placed them down next to everyone’s dishes. i ate a lot of food after this very aesthetic picture taken by jessie Previous Next I’ve always enjoyed potlucks and picnics. Sharing food is a way of sharing your culture and an intimate part of yourself, also it is a good excuse to eat a lot. Study breaks like these also remind me to take a breather in the middle of MIT’s ever lasting chaos. So remember, every once in a while go outside, get some fresh air. and please touch some grass. Trust me, it does help. P.S. Thank you for all the weekly study breaks Tobi!

Title: Hallo-ME-en
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: As you’ve all probably gleaned by now, I’m pretty cool. And like any cool person, my favorite holiday is Halloween. You get the emo, you get the drag, you get the candy, you get the parties–case in point. Yet like all good loves, Halloween and I have had a rocky relationship over the past 20 years.⁠01 Now experiencing another one leaving us behind, and with nothing but the imminent disasters of a Boston winter to look forward to, I find myself looking back through photo albums and Facebook pages to reflect on all of my Halloweens past. So, here I present a photo chronology of all of my past Halloween costumes: 2006-2007: Do babies do Halloween? I don’t know. It would be cute! But regardless there are no photos of me at baby Halloween and I do not know what I was. 2008 – Spiderman I’m fairly certain I wore this Spiderman costume many times, and I can see why! Unfortunately I was cutest as a toddler, and that is very apparent here. If only Marvel had seen this before casting Tom Holland. I’ve been Spiderman. 2009 – Boxer Do I like boxing? No. Do I remember wearing this? No. Do I have perfect form? Yes. 2010-2016 – Unknown?? As an overly angsty elementary schooler, I went through a good number of years as an anti-Halloween guy, mostly for attention. I think one year I was a vampire, but the rest I didn’t dress up at all. Most of the time I would stay back from trick-or-treating to pass out Halloween candy. In 5th grade, though, I went full anti-establishment and just wrote “Costume” on a t-shirt as an act of protest. Looking back, quite possibly the most annoying thing I’ve ever done. At the time? Camp and iconic. 2017 – Rick I had barely seen Rick and Morty by the time I was in 6th grade, but Spirit Halloween had the wig, I wanted to do face paint, and what better way to cover my prepubescent unibrow than with an over-the-top fake one! Also, clock the Woodstock Vans that I wore 24/7 in 6th grade for some reason? In middle school we had dances on/around Halloween every year, so I did fully show up to my 6th grade gym in this, crushed a couple Snickers bars, and danced to Lip Gloss by Lil Mama. 2018 – Bob Ross I don’t have a photo of this one, which is tragic because I ATE in the wig. I went through a very big and genuine Bob Ross phase in 7th grade because it helped me fall asleep, and then he was started to become a pop culture figure for Gen Z, so I pulled out this timely classic. 2019 – Cow This is, unironically, my favorite photo of me ever taken. I use it as my profile picture for everything still, even 7 years later. My mom wanted to get a photo of me for Halloween, and somewhere between all of the photos of me smiling, we got this crazy one where I’m looking pissed straight at the camera. I thought (think, honestly) the rubber utters were the funniest thing. It might have also been inspired by MOO! by Doja Cat because I was very into that at the time, but I can’t confirm if these are causal or correlated cow events. 2021 – E-Girl I don’t know if words can do this justice. My girlfriend Ramona and I floated the idea of doing a Halloween costume contest with our friends just so we had a reason to show people our hilarious idea. We pulled into an H&M, and by the end of the day two baddies were born: an E-boy and an E-girl. What is not accentuated in this photo is how short that plaid skirt sat on my legs and how thick my mascara was. I guess you can count this night as my emo phase? 2023 – Patrick Bateman Senior year of high school, my friends and I drove an hour away to a haunted corn maze. This was bad. Not because of a lack of fun or anything, but instead because I was dressed up as notoriously crazy but undoubtedly sexy Patrick Bateman from American Psycho (about 2 years before it became a trend, btw), yet every single employee at the corn maze kept calling me Harry Potter (which why would Harry Potter have a full suit and a plastic poncho??). 2026 – Jacob Black Flash forward to this year. For the past month, a group of friends on my dorm floor and I have been watching every single Twilight movie. So when the topic of Halloween costumes came up, there was naturally only one thing we could do (we even convinced our GRA)! For reference, I absolutely hate Jacob and am 100% Team Edward. However, it both made more sense for me to be Jacob and would be funnier if my friend Meg H. ’29 was Edward. It initially was just going to be a little bit, but last night we decided to take some creative liberties and do a photoshoot outside in the EC Courtyard. The cast(?) is as follows: Aiden H. ’28 – Jacob Black Meg H. ’29 – Edward Cullen Lauren W. ’28 – Bella Swan Fatimeh A.G. ’27 – Alice Cullen Mack C. Title: How I Won a Costume Contest
Author: Leya E. '30
Article Content: I love Halloween. It’s the only time of year where it’s socially acceptable to put an enormous amount of effort into your outfit. And put an enormous amount of effort into my outfit, I did! Let me take you back to days of Halloweens past. I have always been a bit of a Halloween tryhard. In my junior year of high school I was the best Sanrio character of all time, Cinnamoroll! Then senior year I was the second best Sanrio character, Kerokerokeroppi.⁠01 But this year I decided that I no longer wanted to be cute. I wanted to be scary! Well scary and cute. So I went as the Queen of Hearts! I also put a lot more work into this year’s Halloween costume than my past ones. The last two were mostly just closet cosplays⁠02 and I only made small pieces like Cinnamoroll’s ears, but this time I got the crazy idea in my head to try and make all of it! So here’s a totally accurate list of all the steps I took to make my super cool costume and super win a costume contest. Step 1. Goodwill! Obviously the best place to gather materials for a costume. I took a little solo trip to the Goodwill in Central Square and scoured the aisles for materials. The main problem is that for the Queen of Hearts you really need red clothes and I simply do not own anything that is red. So that was my main goal. I also wanted a black skirt so I could do the fun layering stuff you’ll see later. It seemed like everything was too big or too small until I found a red cropped hoodie and some sort of very long cardigan. And I knew that somehow I could make something of it. Step 2. Glue? Originally I had the ambitious idea to sew the parts of my costume together, but quickly was too hosed to do anything other than use glue. But what glue? I was walking around Concord Market⁠03 and found Elmer’s Glue All. I had never used it before, but it claimed to glue cloth so that was good enough for me! Step 3. Deck of Cards! Throughout my short time here at MIT I have already been exposed to so many decks of cards. There’s HackMIT cards, Coop cards⁠04 , quant cards, just so many different cards! Which is lucky for me, because I needed a deck of cards for my costume! I used a free deck I had gotten from The Coop at Academic Expo because they were the closest to a “traditional” deck that I had. Step 4. Put it together! I played around with the pieces I’d gotten from Goodwill for a little to figure out how I was gonna put them together, and discovered that the black skirt I got was actually a black dress, which made layering a lot easier. I also decided to cut the hoodie part off of the hoodie so it was mostly just like a cropped sleeve thingy. It’ll make sense when you see it. I was more open to altering the red parts of the outfit because I am not a fan of wearing the color red in non-Halloween contexts, and also I really liked the black dress once I discovered that it was a dress. Intermission: Run to Target Related to the fact that I do not like wearing the color red in non-Halloween contexts, I remembered right before Fall Fest⁠05 that I simply did not own any red makeup. So I had to run to Target to get some before it was all gone. It was the most expensive part of my costume. Back to Putting it Together! Once I had the makeup I needed I could return to focusing on putting my outfit together. I camped out in the 2e lounge⁠06 and laid out everything. I was going to glue cards to the collar of my red shirt thingy, the bottom of the red cardigan(which I was using as a skirt), and also to a belt I found! I also decided that I wanted cards to come from behind the dress, and used the severed hood to create that effect! I left it to dry overnight, and decided to indulge in some impromptu Disney karaoke which turned into Just Dance for some reason. Don’t question it. Step 5. Remember That Your Costume is a Queen and Should Probably Have a Crown I realized after finishing everything else that I forgot to make a crown. After searching Pinterest for a few minutes I found a tutorial for making a crown out of cards, and tried to do that, and it actually turned out well! Success! Step 6. Attempt to do Spooky Makeup Pinterest is really great and had a lot of good makeup ideas, so I smashed them up to create something interesting that I could probably do with the help of my newly acquired red eyeshadow. Step 7. Put the Costume on! I put on my entire costume and uh oh it kept falling apart! Apparently Glue All can’t actually glue all. The cards I attached to my belt kept falling off but everything else was sticking and I still managed to get some good pictures so it was fine. Costumes are not always made to be reworn. Step 8. Profit In my dorm we had trick or treating in specific rooms from 4-6, and I happily went and collected all my candy. At 6, the costume contest started! And of course, as you can tell from the title of this post, I won! Okay there are a couple of caveats with this. I won the specific Most Creative category …there were only like 5 people who entered the entire contest. BUT WHO CARES! A WIN IS A WIN! And I suppose I’ve kept you waiting long enough, here’s my costume! As well as some of the other costumes I saw! the belt was already falling apart but its ok I hate blue lock but the costume is fire Where'd he get that hand from... This is sick as hell my prize for winning the contest! Previous Next I hope you all had a happy and safe Halloween, and I wish all of you submitting your early apps the best of luck!

Title: Halloweekend
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content: ‘Tis Halloweekend, a highly anticipated occasion for college students. Fortunately, I’m in college at a time when Halloween mostly falls on the weekend: last year it was on Friday, this year it’s a Saturday, and I believe next year it’s on a Sunday. Not only does this mean a whole weekend full of fun and spooky festivities, but it also means you can enjoy said festivities without too much worry over the greater terrors of exams and problem sets. There’s been a lot to look forward to this Halloweekend. First, IFC⁠01 organized a combined fundraiser for breast cancer research and house-decorating competition among frats. My frat also threw a party on Friday night. With both of these events coming up, we knew we had to lock in on decorations. So, during this past week leading up to Halloweekend, a few of my fellow brothers and I formed the “Halloween committee” to begin decorating the house. We started with lighting, keeping it to mostly red and purple for spooky vibes. It paired really nicely with our front door, which reminds me of the Red Room from The Haunting of Hill House.⁠02 We also ratchet-strapped a projector to the side of one of our fire escape terraces so that we could project onto the sidewalk. Spooky red and purple lighting The projector. It looks precarious but I assure you it was very secure. "Zetasylum" was the name of our party Previous Next Now, for the main attraction: we wanted to have a choir of singing pumpkins! This part was done almost entirely by the amazing Cal R. ’28, our chief handyman. Once we had the pumpkins arranged on some hay bales, Cal set up a hidden projector connected to a Mac mini running QLab.⁠03 From his iPad, he adjusted the projections to fit each pumpkin’s shape and position. Then, through preset animations, they were able to sing several Halloween classics. Check out this video of the pumpkins singing Michael Jackson’s “Thriller”! To top off the exterior, we made spiderwebs out of white netting. Aside from the pumpkins, this was probably my favorite addition. Cal testing the singing pumpkins The fully-decorated exterior! Previous Next On the inside, we replaced the first-floor lightbulbs with some cool flickering ones, then draped some black fabric across the ceiling. Near the entryway, we hung a white curtain and added fake bloodstains and bloody handprints. Our basement setup, featuring a mural that I painted last year Previous Next After all that hard work, the house was at last decorated and in full Halloween spirit. And then we had our party! I dressed up as Scooby-Doo (and by that I mean that I bought an oversized Scooby-Doo hoodie that I can and will wear outside of Halloween). Dylan N. ’28 and me! It’s been awesome seeing all the people, dressed up in their costumes, stopping to take pictures in front of our house. I love Halloween, with all the fright and creativity it brings out in people. I’m sad to see the end of Halloweekend and October in general. I haven’t watched nearly enough horror movies⁠04 for my liking.

Title: Everything Works Out in the End
Author: Richard O. '28
Article Content: College application season is here, and with that often comes the tumultuous fear about what life after high school might look like. Having gone through the college application cycle myself three years ago, I often think back to the fears I had around this time about what my future would look like and where I would end up going. Back then, I had this perfect image of what my college experience would be, what I would do, and where I would go, but if things didn’t go as planned, I was afraid of what would happen otherwise. It got to a point where I put so much energy into perfecting my application that I needed someone like Leanne ’30 in her blog to tell me to just submit it. But even after submitting, I still felt anxious about how my future would turn out at the time and spent my days asking myself whether I’d get in or if I would actually like the schools I applied to or what my career would even look like if I didn’t. And for me, if there was one piece of advice that I always ignored from the adults around me, it was the statement “everything always works out” followed by a sentence like “you’ll be fine no matter where you go or what you do”. Because to me, these adults didn’t know my future any better than I did. They didn’t know what my plans were or what I needed to achieve them. So the sentence felt like a promise that no one could keep because no one can see the future. Now, 3 years down the line, I’ve started to realize that maybe those adults at the time were on to something with their favorite cliche sentences. Despite not being in my shoes and living my experiences, there is something about valuing the perspective that everything happens in a way that just works out that they saw that makes going about big decisions so much more relieving. Because when you think about it, a life in which everything happens the way you think it will would be a boring one. Instead of experiencing all the story options, everything would be a scripted plan that already sits in your head. People don’t (usually) watch movies knowing the whole plot already because you lose the fun of experiencing the story for the first time. And in that same way, I think that as the college application cycle takes place this year, there’s an appreciation to be had for all the possibilities that your life can take on in these next few months. Because no matter where you are or where you go, you’ll always have an opportunity to shape your life into a story that is exciting and unexpected – and that I think is one of the most beautiful parts about being human. So if you’re stressed about your essays, or getting into the perfect school, or what the future holds for you, just take a minute to breathe and appreciate everything you’ve done to get to where you are. And imagine everything you can continue to accomplish in this world just by being you. In the grand scheme of things, the college you go to doesn’t even define your potential and the things you can do for the world. Only you do. And you have a lifetime after college to see the many ways in which that can happen. A song that explains this message a lot more simply and beautifully

Title: hit submit and go frolic in the leaves
Author: Leanne F. '30
Article Content: MIT’s EA deadline is tomorrow, Nov 1. Many of you have probably already submitted, but I know there are a large subset of you who have not (already getting into the MIT procrastination mindset i see). I applied through regular decision, but I went through the same cycles of panic that many of yall probably are going through. I over-edited my essays, ended up hating the new versions, gave up and just submitted the old versions, then completely missed the deadline to submit my research and art portfolio. I had a crashout (but tbh it was pretty minor because I didn’t expect to like MIT anyways), then simply moved on. Which was probably the best thing I could have done. For my friends who are finishing up their applications, you most probably fall into two categories. Here’s my unsolicited advice: If … you’ve finished long ago and are scrutinizing every word you’ve written, thinking crap, these suck, maybe I should rewrite everything. Then you submit and realize you forgot a period and your grammar was wrong and the order of your activities could have been better… Do a last thorough check of everything. Make sure you aren’t missing the important things, and just hit submit. There are probably an infinite amount of small changes you can make that might make your essays marginally better or worse, but also they probably won’t affect much. I agonized over every word and sentence structure, worrying about what it might say about my character. Ima be honest, I doubt a singular adjective change is what got me into MIT! Consider setting a 1-hr timer for yourself to finalize everything, and make yourself submit instead of obsessing over every small detail. Then get yourself a treat, stretch your back, and do some jumping jacks because you deserve it and your neck probably hurts from all that sitting :) If… you’ve just gotten started on your essays and realized you have a ton of work to get done today… bestie… lock in and take a breather! Sit, grab a fun drink, and grind those essays out. I wouldn’t miss your last Halloween just because you need to write essays, though. PLEASE take at least an hour out of your day to go out with your friends and traverse the streets of your neighborhood or city for the last time, because it’ll never be the same again. On my last Halloween at home, I walked through all the same streets I’d walked through for the past decade of my life, seeing the same familiar decorations families had taken out every year. My costume was super lame, scrapped together with a disposable lab coat and goggles from my lab. But I still caught the halloween vibes, frolicked with my friends, and ate a ton of candy. An extra hour of essay writing won’t make or break your application, but that extra hour of halloween festivities with your friends will be something you really treasure in the coming years. …AND I SEE THAT CLAUDE/GEMINI/GPT TAB ON YOUR COMPUTER. CLOSE IT RIGHT NOWWW. NOWWW. NO MATTER how tempting it is to use AI to help write your essays, I promise you. You are not improving your chances by using AI. I can’t speak for admissions but I would bet all my fingers and toes that they would much rather read “bad” human writing than the formulaic word salad slop from AI. If you’ve submitted, congratulations! These essays are not an easy feat. NOW STOP THINKING ABOUT YOUR MIT APPLICATION AND GO FROLIC IN THE FALL LEAVES (if you have them, in San Diego we just had rocks) AND GO PUT ON A COSTUME AND HANG OUT WITH YOUR FRIENDS AND HAVE A JOLLY TIME. A year from now, you will be somewhere. You might be at MIT, or at another college, or working a job, or you’re taking a gap year to explore the world. Maybe you’ll be sitting on a log eating burritos with bearded dragons in Queensland. No one knows, and I think that uncertainty is a beautiful thing. That uncertainty also not something to worry over right now! A year ago, I remember that I imagined myself down the river at Harvard, laying in the fall leaves. Turns out I liked MIT a lil better. And, yesterday, I found myself laying in the fall leaves on Kresge lawn! I’ve unexpectedly found home elsewhere. My point is, things change, you change, but in the end, you’ll figure it out no matter where you go. SO! What did my Friday of halloweekend at MIT actually look like? my bestie who visited from dartmouth! a cat I saw while trick or treating down the infinite Will and his k-hat our baristas at latte lab making drinks! us after watching nightmare on elm street tasting coffee beans in a pourover at latte lab Work in progress of my staph face mask. I added flagella later and cleaned it up cus its a lil messy lol Previous Next I finished my PSETS early for once I skipped recitation (oops) to carve pumpkins and trick or treat around the infinite I had a jolly time struggling with a singular Friday Problem Solving question with my lovely physics group in 8.02 (electricity and magnetism) I made cookie butter and maple hojicha drinks with Latte Lab (MIT’s coffee club) during Fall Fest, our annual fall festival on Kresge lawn I sat in the grass in the leaves under the sun with my friends, listening to a busker sing Hey There Delilah from Plain White T’s (one of my fav songs!!!) while eating chicken noodle soup and apple cider donuts I made a salmonella halloween mask in the Simmons craft room with blogger Ellie and some other friends I ate three insomnia cookies and went to Spooky Skate at Johnson Ice rink I frat hopped with my friends as they all got shut down in like 15 minutes lol I laughed at my friend Will’s k-hat costume because everyone thought i looked like a… green phallic object rather than a k-hat I was reunited with my bestie from San Diego who came down from Dartmouth! We traversed the freezing harvard bridge back to MIT and watched Nightmare on Elm’s street. today(on halloween!) I tried some specialty pour overs with some cool Latte Lab people, and I’m writing this at my favorite good vibes cafe, Flour! Happy halloween!

Title: fall is the best season
Author: Hala K. '29
Article Content: Fall is the best season and that’s not opinions based. You get to pull out all of your staple pieces – a loose leather jacket, your favorite cardigan, maybe some cute rain boots. The weather is perfect so you don’t need to think about how a bulky jacket and thick gloves will mess up your outfit or how the humidity will frizz up your hair. All of your favorite restaurants are adding back the seasonal items you’ve waited a whole year for: Flour’s coconut caramel hot chocolate (please try this if you haven’t already, I actually think about it every single day), Trader Joe’s butternut squash mac and cheese, and of course, the dining hall’s pumpkin flavored ice cream. Though most importantly, THE TREES! Every time you step outside, orange and red foliage canopies over you and the places you walk by every single day seem to be significantly more aesthetic. I have taken at least one picture every single time I have left my room for the past 2 weeks. So, here’s some clear evidence as to how much prettier the fall is compared to any other season. Note: I’ve taken most of these pictures when I’m already late for something so recognize that in real life, it is 10x more pretty. the view immediately outside of New Vassar. look at how pretty the leaves on the ground are!! THE GREAT DOME! I mean easily one of the prettiest sights on campus and now the trees even have a bit of red to them hayden library courtyard! the whole time I studied here, leaves were falling from the trees and it was so so pretty another picture outside of new vassar – i love the yellow and green trees with the bright blue sky behind it this is the east side of campus with the MIT List Visual Arts Center to the left – I just loved how the sun kept peeking in from behind the trees i’ve never even PROCESSED that building 34 is this cute. i love the all glass look of the building next to the big yellow tree another hayden studying one (ignore my greys anatomy + 2.001 combo). The trees make the charles sparkle even more than normal i swear a book sale in harvard square this weekend! flowers are to spring as books are to fall (as fall is to being the best season) sunrise from my dorm window! the field is so busy during the fall so it’s always fun to look out and watch whatever is going on. it’s also cool that I casually have a pretty view of the boston skyline the picture speaks for itself. on my walk to a cafe today – this is a scene straight out of gilmore girls. LOOK AT THE LANTERN! also, the trees are already starting to lose their leaves which makes me sad and finally, as I write this, this is the view from my cafe’s window Fall is the best season – I rest my case.

Title: how to become paulie bleeker
Author: Emily P. '28
Article Content: First things first, if you haven’t already seen Juno (2007), please go & do that first. Ok, so now that we are all on the same page about how awesome this movie is, let’s get started. To become Paulie Bleeker, you will need: 1 maroon t-shirt with a dancing elk condors graphic on it, preferably cotton 1 pair of yellow running shorts yellow headband and wristband crew socks running shoes I sourced my t-shirt, shorts, and yellow fabric (which was harvested from a yellow t-shirt) from the local Boomerangs and Central Square Goodwill. 01 how to put a dancing elk condors graphic on a t-shirt There are a lot of ways to go about putting a graphic on a t-shirt, including but not limited to: screen printing, heat press vinyl, good ol’ fabric paint, embroidery (machine or hand, but you’d be crazy to do the latter for Paulie Bleeker’s shirt), and appliqué. Believe it or not, you can actually do any of the techniques I mentioned above through the MIT Makerspaces, but I decided to go with appliqué because I like the look of it. Appliqué just means putting smaller pieces of fabric on larger pieces of fabric to make a design. The tricky thing is cutting out the fabric. Serious textile artists who make really intricate designs tend to use electronic fabric cutting machines; last I checked, we don’t have one of these on campus, and I wasn’t planning on spending my weekend precisely trimming out tiny letters and a smug-looking condor. We do, however, have a crap ton of laser cutters, and laser cutters can cut fabric. We run into problem #2. How to transfer the graphic onto the shirt and get it to stay there? Yes, I can sew it on, but again, I wasn’t planning on spending my weekend precisely sewing on tiny—you get the point. A little concerned about whether I will be able to realize my dream of becoming Paulie Bleeker in time for Halloween, I start digging around the MAD⁠02 textile lab and find this mysterious roll of paper labeled “Iron This Side Feather Weight hotfixadhesive.com.” After some googling, I came up with the following game plan. Cut out feather weight hotfix adhesive to size. My graphic was about 9” x 9”, so I cut out a square about 10” x 10”. Iron onto yellow fabric, trim to size. square of hotfix adhesive and square of fabric ironing adhesive to fabric Previous Next Flip over to the other side of the fabric. Cover with painter’s tape. This will help prevent scorching the cotton, and if you leave a ½” border, will also help secure the piece down on the laser cutter bed. adding painter’s tape to the other side, with extra tape border tape border Previous Next Place in laser cutter, blue tape side up, hotfix adhesive side down. The fabric should be safely sandwiched between. Import your graphic, double-check the sizing, placement, and cut settings; cross your fingers, curl your toes, hold your breath, and cut! 03 fabric taped to laser cutter bed test your settings on scrap first omgomgomg Previous Next Marvel at the power of technology. Carefully remove painter’s tape. You’ll be ironing the fabric, and painter’s tape is a no-no. Flip to the other side, the one with the hotfix adhesive. You want to remove the adhesive paper wherever you want the fabric to stick to your shirt. You could technically just separate the pieces at this point and position them by hand, but I wanted an exact placement of the Dancing Elk Condors graphic to be as Paulie Bleeker as possible, not some foolish doppelganger who got the spacing between the letters wrong. there’s a paper backing and then the adhesive. be careful not to remove the adhesive from the fabric! Carefully transfer your graphic to your t-shirt, which should be waiting patiently on the ironing board (good practice to also iron out your maroon shirt before you add the graphic). I slid a piece of paper under my graphic, sandwiched it with another sheet of paper to secure, flipped, and slid the graphic onto my maroon shirt so that the yellow was facing up again and the hotfix adhesive was on the bottom. Iron away. I placed some muslin in between to prevent accidentally burning the cotton, and ironed for a good while to make sure it was really stuck on. Cross fingers, curl toes, and hold breath. Peel back the negative. i'm so scared omgomgomg Previous Next become Paulie Bleeker becoming paulie bleeker Previous Next

Title: i have never been this unprepared for a test
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: so today i wake up at 9:30 even though it’s a wednesday, because i have to leave the dorm by 9:50 in order to walk across campus to get to the z⁠01 for my fencing class. i take a slightly diverted route by the walker memorial, where i start a stopwatch to time how long it takes. i get a little held up at the check-in at the z because something is wrong with my id, but i note that it takes ~8 minutes to get from walker to the z. fencing is fun. i am a bit sleepy – i didn’t sleep the best; kept waking up at times. today we start off with stretches, then some footwork, and then we get some equipment on. yay! we all get a helmet, a glove, and a saber. we learn punch-cut and then mix that with a lunge, and then we take turns doing this attack on the instructor and on some dummies. we start wrapping up at 10:52; i would guess i walk out the door at 10:54. go down stairs walk out doors walk eastside to walker this is why i was timing myself – i wanted to make sure i had enough time to get from pe to my chem midterm in walker. luckily because of mit time⁠02 i got there in time (like 11:02) and had time to use the restroom and whatnot. i write my name on the paper test in front of me. at 11:06, “you can start the exam!” i open the test wtf wtf wtf how the heck do i do this ??? ?? what. okay lemme start here. wow this seems annoying go to next problem okay maybe you do this ?? this seems so sus wtf am i doing let’s move on holy crap i only have 30 minutes left? oh my god how do you do this i swear this wasn’t covered in class wtf is this ????? FIVE MINUTES cries out the proctor holy crap. holy crap last minute calculation wtf is going on oh my god genuinely this might be the worst i have ever done on a test at 12:06, time is up. the proctor comes to pick up our tests, joking “don’t worry, guys, i’ll rescue you”. weakly i say “i think i need rescuing”. i stand up out of my seat in a daze and walk over to jsin. “i think i’m cooked,” i say. “me too,” she says. we walk out of the testing room “how do you do question 3?” i ask. she says some things that i had no clue about. wtf??? “i didn’t know that,” i say. “wait that was the only one i knew,” she says. we commiserate as we walk towards east campus. “can i get my lunch so we can eat together?” i ask. “sure,” she says. i get my leftover chipotle from the fridge and then we walk up to florey,⁠03 where she opens her chili. i try not to crash out too much. we talk about the arrangement jsin did last night instead of studying for the test. i hold in my crash out. she eats chili. she looks at her phone and says “oh there’s free cake in the lounge fridge!” we eat cake. it’s pretty good! strawberry and whipped cream… delicious. i arrange a time for us to draw together; i really want to do a self portrait because i haven’t drawn in a while by now it is 12:44 and i am no longer losing it (at least, not as much). in high school i never saw the time left on the clock and panicked, but on this test that’s what i did. such a bad feeling. aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa i’m in diffeq lecture now. i have a spanish in class essay at 2:30. aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa

Title: Chasing Butterflies
Author: Allison E. '27
Article Content: It’s an autumn evening in 2019–my first year in my high school’s marching band–and the clock is ticking towards midnight on our darkened school bus. Heads slump against precariously stacked saxophone cases, weighed down by a long day of football pep songs and field performances. As the bus turns off the freeway back towards school, the sound of traffic gives way to the soft rumble of the engine. Just as the wheels make their final turn, however, the quiet is shattered by a single bellowing voice: “2, 4, 6, 8, WHO DO WE APPRECIATE?” Heads snap awake as if they’d never been asleep, and the one shout becomes many, all in unison. “BUS DRIVER, BUS DRIVER, YEAHHH BUS DRIVER!” By now, the entire band is awake, and the shouts continue even stronger. “ARISTOTLE, SOCRATES, PELOPONNESIAN WAR! (WAR!)” “X-SQUARED, Y-SQUARED, H-2-S-O-4! (4!)” “WHO FOR? WHAT FOR? WHO THE HELL WE CHEERING FOR?” “BUS DRIVER, BUS DRIVER, YEAHHH BUS DRIVER!” Incoherent yelling ensues as the bus doors open. The quiet is now broken, and lively banter bubbles up again as we unload instruments through the front gate. This is the thank you cheer my high school’s marching band shouts after returning from every football game or performance, whether it’s 4:00 PM or midnight, whether we’ve won or lost, and whether the bus driver has heard it twenty times or none at all. It’s such a small moment–30 seconds, repeated so often that you forget it’s there. But when I think back on high school, it’s the moment that sits at the very top of my shelf of memories, because in many ways it’s the best monument I have to my 9th grade self, my 12th grade self, and all the years in between. The first bus driver cheer of my freshman year happened before I ever felt like I belonged in marching band. In fact, that same week I was actively thinking about quitting–I didn’t feel like I’d made new friends, I was too awkward to participate in the more ridiculous banter, and I couldn’t replicate the enthusiasm everyone else seemed to have for the band. I spent a lot of time quite literally sitting in the corner, feeling out of place and just observing. When it came to the bus driver cheer, however, I didn’t have to feel like I belonged to take part in the tradition. All I needed to do was to be on that bus. The lyrics were silly, the rhymes were catchy, and the yelling was all a bit intoxicating. But as funny as the Greek history references were, the best thing about it was the camaraderie. The camaraderie of shouting yourself hoarse with others, and of feeling so in-sync that you can’t make out your own voice from the group’s. You don’t even need to know the people around you to feel it. After all, connection is what songs and chants are meant for, and the bus driver cheer did exactly that. It gave me something to share. It made me a part of the group. It convinced me to stay long enough to fall in love with marching band, and kept me from missing out on the most fulfilling part of my high school experience. And then bam. COVID. Unfortunately, marching band–an activity spent blowing air out of your mouth and into your surroundings–is… notably difficult to do during a global pandemic. So is getting into a crowded school bus and shouting in unison. As you can probably guess, lockdown turned our marching band into a shadow of itself for two years, and the bus driver cheer went into stasis. By the time restrictions loosened again, three class years had graduated, and three more had moved up to replace them without learning the cheer. Only a handful of us still knew the lyrics. But the bus driver cheer absolutely could not die, so in the first few weeks we went on a crusade to make sure that everyone in the band learned it. We passed around lyrics, whispered reminders from seat to seat, and double checked that even our shyest underclassmen knew what was happening. All it took was one bus ride for the loudest and most enthusiastic amongst us to join in (band kids will be band kids). But as the semester continued, even our shyest frosh were shouting it with more and more energy, until they were practically as loud as our seniors. And so the camaraderie of that tradition was revived for another generation. This story was the first half of my Common App essay⁠01 , more or less my senior thesis on who I was and what I valued most. Four years later, as a senior once again, I’ve been thinking about the version of Allison that wrote that essay. Am I the same person? Am I different? Certainly this is still the story that present-day me thinks of when imagining the word “community.” It feels so short-lived when I look back on it, as if it were a snapshot of people caught together in a crosswalk–paths intersecting half by chance, half by proximity, then continuing on in different directions. But a snapshot, as brief and ephemeral as it is, still captures the image of a much larger subject. At the risk of sounding corny, that larger subject is less a crosswalk than it is a tree. It’s a community that lives, and grows, and blossoms just the same as a tree. A community with roots sunk so deep into the past and new branches reaching far enough into the future that it can’t fade with time. A community where each person is just one small leafy shoot, but together the years of those before build the foundation for years of those to come, with leadership and mentorship and traditions flowing upwards through the veins of one person to the next. A community grows and renews with a larger purpose. Instead of pouring energy into making springtime flowers bloom, it pours its dedication into putting on a musical show, or building a robot, or winning a competition. And that community is held together by the structure of that purpose–by the rehearsals and meetings and practices that work towards it. If you go to those rehearsals, and you are working towards the purpose, you are part of that tree, no questions asked. And there’s a comfort to knowing you’re a part of it. Part of something so large. Something so solid. Something with a past and a future and a purpose. That’s what community feels like to me. All throughout high school, marching band and Science Olympiad and cross country and math team were practically my entire world. They were the most fulfilling parts of my life, and I absolutely knew it, so when I came to MIT, I was ready to plunge headfirst into every community I could find–clubs, dorm life, music groups–anything and everything. And that’s what I did. I jumped in with enthusiasm, and started to feel at home with various communities on campus. At the same time, though, I was also discovering another facet of life at MIT: college friends. The friends who you stay up talking with until 5:00 am, and who are willing to indulge your dumbest ideas and join you on the most ridiculous adventures. I’ve had friends before, of course, but something about college and living together and the pure silliness of MIT made it different. It was intoxicating. Unfortunately, our time is finite, over the course of freshman fall I found myself having to choose between my friends and the communities I’d started becoming a part of. And I ended up almost always choosing my friends. I spent late nights having absurd conversations in study rooms, poured organizational energy into group shenanigans, and invested emotionally in these relationships. This came at the cost of my engagement with the new clubs I had joined, and even though community was so baked into my sense of identity, I continued making those choices. But as freshman fall turned into freshman spring, my friends got busier, classes got tougher, and it became harder and harder to spend time together. The spontaneous moments studying in the library or eating dinner started dissolving, and it became more difficult to wrangle people into a cooking project or late night discussion. Unlike with my clubs, there were no guaranteed weekly meetings or regularly scheduled events to rely on, and as the loneliness began to hit my mental health I started rethinking my decision to prioritize my friendships over everything else. I wrote this in the midst of that fear: I don’t think I’ve ever depended so much on people for my own happiness before, and it’s scary. I’ve depended on institutions–on solid things with schedule and structure and the cyclic constancy of meetings that will always happen because people see it as their responsibility. But I’ve never depended so wholly on this amorphous thing that is a group of friends, each with their own lives that intersect in different ways, where the schedules don’t exist and every. single. moment. has to be chased, and caught, and held like a butterfly in nervous, shaky hands. I feel like my happiness is built upon a marshland, where the currents flow underfoot and the ground sinks beneath you and you never know where your next step will land. I want the solidity of a boardwalk, with its symmetrical planks and its strictly dictated path. I want something I know will be there every time I put my foot down for the next step, and for every other step in this one direction that we’re all headed in together. But oh, I want the butterfly more. I want the warmth of the marsh and the joy of a thousand things breathing all at different times and with different sounds. I am standing in the marsh scared shitless by the shifting ground, but I’m also in love with the life here. I just don’t know how to stay on my feet. Communities are usually stable things. There’s so much security that comes from knowing that meetings or rehearsals or just time with “your people” are regularly scheduled, and people will show up. It’s difficult to pull communities apart, because their seams are all stitched with a common purpose and a sense of responsibility to a common goal. The fluidity of friendships is so much harder to navigate, especially when every event to be planned starts feeling like a massive balancing act. You schedule it at a time when everyone’s awake, but there isn’t much going on. You remind people individually with just enough wheedling to lure them from their psets, but not so much that they feel coerced. You make sure enough people join that everyone feels it was worth their time, or else they’ll be harder to convince for the next group activity. When you do get the chance to hang out, you can’t let the conversation turn towards psets or sleep schedules, or plans the next day–otherwise people will start thinking about reasons to leave. You provide food, or a planned activity, or good conversation, and string them one after another with as little space in between for possible departures. Because each moment together must be chased. Must be caught. Must be held like a butterfly in nervous, shaky hands. There are some groups that have the best of both worlds. They’re both circles of friends and communities in their own right–friends that live together, or take classes together, or have some regular guarantee of encounters. I’ve spent a long time trying to manufacture these aspects of community within my own group of friends. And I think there’s merit in that effort. Community has been one of the most important and fulfilling parts of my life, and turning my friends into a community would bring that feeling back into my life. But chasing butterflies is also an exhausting, Sisyphean task. And more importantly, I’ve begun to realize that community is not the be all and end all for this sense of kinship. Most obviously, friendships usually come with a deeper level of connection. With just friends, there’s no artificial scaffolding holding our relationship together at a few scattered contact points–we show up with our entire person and connect with our entire person. We aren’t trapped in conversations revolving around just music, or just math, or just “the thing” our community does. We can talk about linguistic drift for three hours on a random weeknight. We can share our insecurities about our future careers. We can cry for thirty minutes straight, and then we can hug each other, and then we can just sit there and be. I think friendship also comes with a completely different flavor of belonging. In a community, as long as I show up to all the designated activities, I’m accepted as a member. I don’t have to be funny, or interesting, or even that likeable–as long as I’m showing up, I belong. There’s reassurance in that fact, but there’s also a shallower sense of belonging. With my friends, it’s worth so much to know that they care about me because they like me as a person, and because they enjoy being around me. I don’t have a job to do or deadlines to hit to be a “contributing member” of an organization; my friends like me for me. They think I’m funny, and they think I’m interesting to talk to, and when shit hits the fan and I don’t have the energy to contribute anything, they’re exactly where they’ve always been–right alongside me. There are so many other dimensions of friendship, and I’m still exploring them. I’m learning how to maintain individual relationships in a world where convenience doesn’t draw us naturally together (shoutout to my friend Miranda for being the role model that I’ve been studying ). But I’m also still partly mourning the loss of a more standard community in my life. Without the stability of belonging to an institution and the perpetuity of a constantly growing organization, I feel so much more unmoored than I did in high school. I wish I was leaving more of a mark on this school–building something that lasts, or helping the people after me build it themselves. Instead I’m still here chasing butterflies, but with less and less energy to do it. Maybe there’s a balance to be found. Perhaps having a job and a workplace and coworkers has some of those community aspects to it, and perhaps outside the whirlwind of MIT there are friendships that don’t require chasing. I suppose I’ll find out in the next few years. In the meantime, though, have I made the right decision for my four years at MIT? I don’t know. I’m happy with where I am now, and I’m more than happy with all the people that are in my life, and I think that’s all I can really ask for.
