works.⁠04 for a few weeks i basically nolife this course⁠05 – i stay up late to watch lectures, i work on a pset during my flight to mit scibowl, i probably ignored some of my schoolwork, etc etc. december 2024: nothing january 2025: nothing february 2025: nothing march 2025: nothing april 2025: nothing may 2025: nothing june 2025: nothing july 2025: nothing august 2025: nothing september 2025: nothing october 2025: nothing november 2025: nothing december 2025: nothing january 2026: nothing february 2026: nothing march 2026: nothing april 2026: nothing may 2026: nothing june 2026: nothing july and august 2026: i decide to try to ase⁠06 out of 6.100A, which means i have to relearn everything that i forgot over the past year and a half. what this boiled down to is i went through the sample exam that they gave us, solving the “write code!” problems and thinking about the multiple choice. i realized that even though i’d forgotten a lot of the syntax, i still remembered a lot of the like thought processes and approaches that are often helpful when programming.⁠07 also i did some of “watch people who are better than me code” which was maybe helpful. not sure. october 2026 (now): i finally do something that’s not “speedrun a class” or “take a test” with coding. whaaaaat so what am i doing? this semester i’m taking a class called 12.004, aka intro to the global carbon cycle. it’s in the earth, atmospheric, and planetary sciences department as one of their 4 intro classes. this class is about all the places that carbon is sequestered and how it moves around, especially in the ocean⁠08 which basically means that it is a class that i think is awesome, because i really like the ocean and i want to work on climate and the carbon cycle is AAAAAA so important. this class is interesting because it combines typical lecture about like theory (right now a lot of chemistry) with a significant computational portion. to illustrate, this week we’ve been working on a pset that has two parts. part one is the theoretical part: one question asks us to “Determine what fraction of nitrogen (N2) is in the atmosphere vs. the ocean,” while the other has us derive an expression for the dissolved oxygen concentration in a hypothetical raindrop over time. this part was deceptively hard for me, but i went to office hours with the professor and then everything made sense! so yay part two is the computational part. basically we are writing some code to do some annoying arithmetic for us as we develop “box models”. what do i mean by a box model? well, here’s a drawing from my notes: yeah there are more detailed ones but i realized i didn’t copy them down but you just abstract different things down to little boxes that interact with each other in simple ways. our first coding project is a two-box model: there is the atmosphere, which has co2, and the ocean, which has dissolved co2, which then reacts with water to form bicarbonate and a proton, and then the bicarb disassociates to form carbonate and another proton. we introduce a bunch of different constraints and eventually end up with a system of 7 equations and 7 unknowns, which we want to solve. the coding part of this is really not intense – or perhaps it is more accurate to say that it isn’t really the focus of the problem solving ?? i looked at the pset before we talked about it in class, and i was confused as to how we were supposed to code something that generated a polynomial in H+ concentration. it turns out we just do that part by hand and end up with a cubic in H+ that we can then solve and then replug into everything else. but we do code a simple root-finder! yippee. back to what the pset wants me to do! part 1 asked us to complete the work we’d done in class by fully finding dic (which stands for dissolved inorganic carbon – basically co2 + hco3- + (co3)2-) given the partial pressure of co2 in the atmosphere. yeah looking back at my code i am not a huge fan of the way i set this up but it’s probably fine??? this was reasonably straightforward i feel. parts 2, 3, and 4 asked me to generate some plots using matplotlib. this was the part that really shocked me – i had actually never used matplotlib ever and had some sort of innate fear of it.⁠09 so it was pretty crazy when (after learning the syntax for how to plot a simple two-axis plot) my code just worked first try it and generated a REAL GRAPH. i was like wtf i texted both my friend scarlet and my little brother to be like holy crap i feel so powerful. this is also what pushed me to write this post! wow look at that plot! ignore the units part 5 was basically the same thing as part 1; just solve a slightly different cubic that is given to us and then plug and solve into the rest of the other equations. we also had to go back and make sure that this works by checking with our answers from part 1. part 6… part 6 stumped me for a while. it is a much different form of question than the other 5 parts: where the other 5 asked to plot or to implement a general solver, part 6 asked us to use the tools we previously came up with and make some assumptions in order to estimate the pco2 of a parcel of water gradually moving northward over the course of a month. what this ends up being like is asking us to make a very simple differential equation numerical solver; i lowkey don’t know if i could have come up with the actual differential equation⁠10 in closed form but i feel like i did good enough. basically my workflow for solving this problem was stare at the question be confused stare harder try to think give up find a chalkboard draw on the chalkboard drawing on chalkboards is really fun. i think this might be a big reason why people decide to do math, just because drawing on chalkboards makes you feel intellectual. but chalkboard was good for writing down ideas! if anyone is working on this very pset rn don’t look at my work it is like a lot wrong the chalkboarding took place from like 9:30 to 10:30pm in a random classroom in building 66; then i went back to tetazoo and watched people play tomodachi life while i typed stuff up. while typing it up i realized that my first initial model made no sense – the answer i got was like lower than it started, when i felt like it should probably be higher. i went to my room because i was very sleepy; i then realized that the reason why my model didn’t make sense is that i didn’t realize that my code also calculated the value of a coefficient that i needed but didn’t know i had. then i went to sleep because it was like 2am i got to watch a wedding while i worked on my pset! so wholesome after i woke up i fixed my code and made some new assumptions, and i think it went well. my actual solution turned out much simpler than what i was initially cooking up; it did kind of feel like i wasted a lot of time thinking, but whatever! it’s fine. i turned in the pset a whole twelve hours before it was due (could have been better but this last problem was hard) and then stopped thinking about it. my final submitted pdf ended up being 8 pages and my code ended up being 223 lines long thoughts on coding i definitely am not the cleanest coder. for example, i think i am missing some modularity, because i have two basically identical functions that just find roots of slightly different functions, but the way i have them set up there’s something internal that’s different, so i just have two copies. with a bit of extra time i could probably make a general root-finder, but this is like not the point of this part of the class i think. i also think i am not particularly efficient? like not like my code is inefficient, I AM inefficient as i write my code. on the other hand i completely understand the satisfaction of having your code work. i kind of felt this while i was reviewing for the ase – it’s really satisfying to see the thing you typed up actually successfully do what it’s supposed to. but also i feel like i am just really not a good programmer and i don’t know if i want to put in the work to become a good programmer⁠11 i did really enjoy this assignment tho! our final project in this class is like this but more detailed and also self-developed – i am excited for it :)

Title: The Incorrect Biological Hypothesis
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: A couple of week’s ago, MIT’s film/cinema club LSC⁠01 hosted a pre-screening of the new hit rom-com “The Love Hypothesis” in 26-100⁠02 for free! I didn’t go (oops!), but I did watch the movie the night it came out on Prime Video.⁠03 If you don’t know, the movie follows the fake-dating, enemies-to-lovers romance between a biology PhD student, Olive, and a biology post-doc, Adam. I think the reason it was chosen as one of MIT’s exclusive pre-screenings is because the movie is very science- and academia-focused. What a mistake! Showing a movie so deeply embedded in scientific practice to a group of scientists is a sure-fire way for the absolute most criticism. And oh my god were there so many errors. Most people talking about the movie are obviously not focused on correct biological practices and instead on the over-six-foot-totally-jacked-genius professor, but trust that I am holding the fort down. To get this off my chest, here is everything (that I can remember) that The Love Hypothesis gets wrong about biology/academia: 1. Olive’s Dorm Early in the movie, Olive is shown to have a very traditional, undergraduate-style dorm room. This is wrong for many reasons. Mostly that if Olive were to live in an undergraduate dorm, she would be an RA and would therefore have a much larger dorm with its own bathroom and kitchenette. However, most likely, Olive would have lived in a graduate dorm, which almost universally have apartment-style housing instead of individual dorm rooms. Eventually, Olive does move out with her friends into an off-campus house, which is more realistic. 2. Lab Bathroom A key scene at the beginning of the movie involves the two main characters meeting in what Adam calls his “lab bathroom”. This is not a thing. First, it is ridiculous to assume that any university has enough funding to have a full bathroom that is out of commission just to have extra lab sinks. Second, this is a total safety hazard to have an extraneous, publicly accessible location with exposure to any biologicals or chemicals. Like, you have to have gloves and all the safety signs and things. Third, most biologicals Adam would be using can’t be poured down a normal sink drain either, but in specialized lab sinks that are specifically hooked to different sewer lines so as to not create mass exposure to random things. 3. That’s not how a Post-Doc works One of the key differences between the book and the movie is that, in the book, Adam is a professor in the biology department, while in the movie he is only a post-doc. The reasoning behind this was to lessen the severity of the power-gap between the characters and reduce stigma. Unfortunately, they forgot to fix every other detail that involves the differences in power between a post-doc and professor. Essentially, the movie just treats Adam as a professor, and calls him a post-doc. He has his own office and laboratory and PhD students (fully not a thing, only professors have this–post-docs work in labs under professors instead). Also, he himself applies and renews his own grants, when again post-docs work under labs where the professor is the main point for funding. He also is the keynote speaker at a large biology conference later in the film (not as hard for a post-doc, but to be the keynote speaker as a post-doc is crazy, when there are full professors with large labs and decades of experience over you that they didn’t pick?). And, most importantly, no post-doc is that hot. Sorry, but if you’re a post-doc, you probably work ~10 hrs/day, 5-6 days a week. When are you getting jacked? Not during lab babe, sorry :( 4. Classes For most of the movie, Olive is a PhD candidate as opposed to a PhD student. This assumes her primary focus is her research and dissertation and not the Master-level classes and thesis required of early-PhD students. Yet, Olive and all of her friends are consistently seen in lectures (which also lowkey have early undergrad-level biology being explained, like the MAP-Kinase pathway). Sure, candidates can take one or two classes, but they have absolutely no reason to except pure interest, and most candidates are interested in their own research instead of learning a new subject. In fact, instead of being in class, Olive should be teaching one, which leads us to… 5. Not a TA Graduate students are typically either required or very very very much want to TA undergraduate classes, as they provide stipends that count towards your probably already-low pay as a full-time PhD. But yet again, Olive and any of her friends having to leave lab to teach is not mentioned. This wouldn’t be that big of a deal considering it would have no impact on the plot, BUT Olive is shown teaching a class for…middle schoolers? When she would have the time or requirement to do this, I don’t know. Also it was a chemistry lab, so like what? 6. Mice Olive works on blood biomarkers to detect pancreatic cancer (we’ll get to this later). As a result, she works on mice. And, in true fashion, she breaks absolutely every safety rule with mice protocols?? Most importantly, the mice are kept in the normal lab on her regular lab bench. This is, of course, not allowed. Mice terminals/rooms are required to be in separate rooms away from the traditional lab to protect the people, the mice, and the other chemicals and biologicals in the lab. Yet every time we see Olive with her mice, they’re just on the bench with other people around running other experiments. 7. PPE (Personal Protective Equipment). Gloves and a lab coat are required to be worn when touching almost anything in a lab, regardless of the lab’s safety level. Even more importantly, gloves and lab coats must be removed when leaving lab so that you don’t contaminate the outside world with anything from the lab. But dur-de-dur, none of these full-grown professors, post-docs, and PhD students follow this rule. There are full scenes where they are walking around in the hallways of the biology building with lab coats and gloves. Danger danger! 8. Working Alone It is known that Olive consistently works alone in the lab on weekends instead of going out and partying (cause she’s not like other girls etc etc.). This isn’t totally uncommon, but it is strange, and typically requires special permission from the PI since it is a safety issue to have people in the lab alone. 9. Transferring to Harvard? A large plot point throughout the movie is Olive trying to get a research position at a lab at Harvard university. This is capital-S strange. People in the movie treat this as “yay you’re getting this super cool opportunity”, which would make sense if she was a research assistant or even post-doc. But as a student, this means fully transferring programs, having to apply to Harvard, and do all that, which normally means you’re having a really negative experience in your current program and are willing to burn a bridge with your current PI over it. They do not acknowledge this. 10. Olive = Elizabeth Holmes Olive works on bio-blood markers as an early detection metric for pancreatic cancer. This is theoretically cool, but someone already did it, honey: Elizabeth Holmes. This is an actual field of study and it is valid, but I can’t help but see a blonde White woman talking about her idea to use blood to test for disease and immediately hear Elizabeth Holmes’ voice.

Title: my classes are exploding
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content: This semester, I’m finally off the credit limit! ⁠01 There’s nothing holding me back >:) And so this semester, I cranked the knob on the firehose ⁠02 to maximum and made the brilliantly horrible choice to register for 7 classes. They are as follows: 8.05: Quantum Mechanics II: I’m now officially a Physics major ⁠03 . I’d taken 8.04 (Quantum Mechanics I) last year, and this just seemed like the natural next step. I did have some mixed feelings about 8.04—I thought that the class was very heavy on algebra and churning numbers—but I hoped that 8.05 would give me a better understanding and appreciation. 8.033: Relativity: Another physics class; I had heard many good things about the lecturer, Scott Hughes, and they did not disappoint—he has a really engaging lecturing style and seems to care a lot about the class. In fact, our class is being recorded for MIT OpenCourseWare, so by the end of the semester, maybe the lectures will be public! 18.901: Introduction to Topology: I was actually really excited about this class. I took Algebra I and II ⁠04 last year, and really enjoyed pure mathematics. I plan to declare a double major in mathematics next semester, and 18.901 is a requirement for the major. Plus, most of my previous math experience was in algebra (which I really like), and I wanted to broaden out to some analysis. 18.404: Theory of Computation: My friend took this class last year and had very high reviews of it. It looked interesting and fit in my schedule, so I added it…and to be honest, in hindsight maybe this is why my schedule exploded so much—when I was selecting classes, my philosophy was “if it fits, I’m taking it”… which looking back, was not a very good philosophy. 21G.402: German II: In high school, I really wanted to learn German. I think I just wanted to learn a language, and chose German arbitrarily because it sounded cool, I guess. I self-studied it on and off for a bit but never got too far because I was not very concentrated in my efforts. Since I had some German knowledge beforehand, I was able to skip to German II. 21G.611: Russian I: I started “learning” Russian about last year, and by “learning” I mean I had two friends who spoke Russian and I would go about asking one of them for insults in Russian to use against the other. Somehow through this I’ve gotten attached to the language, and this semester I resolved to learn more words than “дурак” ⁠05 . 21G.086: 20th Century Ukraine and Russia: Entangled Histories and Identity Politics: All MIT students are required to take a total of 2 CI-H ⁠06 subjects in their first and second years, and this is effectively our writing requirement. This was actually my second choice of CI-H—I had really wanted to take a German film class, but it had gotten unexpectedly cancelled. I had really enjoyed my history class in my senior year of high school, and was sad when we ran out of time to finish our Soviet Union unit; hence, I was excited when I saw this in the course catalogue, especially since it’s pretty relevant today. [Spoiler: I’m not in all of them anymore but somehow, for some reason, possessed by some sort of insanity, at the beginning of the semester I was fully planning to take all of them. When I met with my advisor to confirm my registration before classes started, she had (like a good advisor) expressed concern over my almost-double-the-amount-of-coursework. I therefore promised that I would drop some, but secretly I didn’t plan to. But then I did ¯\_(ツ)_/¯] This is what my schedule during the first week of classes looked like: ahhhhhh …due to some stroke of bad luck (yes yes I’m going to blame it all on luck), my classes all lined up in a row. Here’s what my first day of classes looked like: I biked ⁠07 to Stata Center at 10:30am to get a bagged lunch before sitting in 18.901 for an hour and a half, speedwalking across campus to make it in time for 8.05, where we reviewed the material for 8.04 for one and a half hours, then scarfing down my lunch outside the lecture room (I was lucky that all the physics classes occur in the same room, 6-120, and so I had ten minutes of break where I didn’t have to relocate) before another hour and a half of lecture. Then I had a whopping thirty minutes of break! I sat in the LODGE ⁠08 and responded to some emails. I ended my academic day with an hour of Russian, where we said привет to each other for what seemed like a million times. After a total of 5.5 hours of lecture, most of them consecutively, I felt… great! I was surprised that I had held my concentration intact for such a long time, and I felt so accomplished and productive. I couldn’t wait for my problem sets to come out, so I could feel even more productive by doing them. That Sunday was a beautiful sunny day out, and I spent ten hours sitting in my room, doing my homework. Needless to say (though it was not very needless then and was quite a surprise), it was not sustainable. Although I had felt great at the start, by the end of the first full week of classes, I was getting a bad tension headache everyday from sitting in 4-4.5 hours of lecture in a row for four days in a week, then going home and spending many more hours in a row on problem sets. So I decided that if my brain was not going to overload this semester, I simply had to drop some classes. Yet even so, when I finally mustered up the strength to submit my Class Drop form, I felt some sort of separation anxiety (maybe others will call it Stockholm Syndrome). I’d psyched myself up so hard for seven classes that taking any less felt…not enough. Why did I decide to overload my schedule like this? Surely, a mix of hubris, bad foresight, and that desire to optimize everything in my life. When I was little and learning to write in Chinese, I had those workbooks of characters where you trace out characters in the book. Having been 8 or 9, at the ripe age where one learns about the Industrial Revolution in school history class, I took inspiration from the factories of the 19th century and pretended my Chinese homework was an assembly line—what happened was I wrote a row of the first strokes of some character, then went back and added the second strokes, then the third, until I had completed the page. There were some problems with this—notably, no one writes like that (imagine writing a book by writing the first letters of each word, then the second, then the third, until all your words are complete). And notably, it’s not the way you should learn to write—as a consequence, I’m still illiterate. I think the same mindset that made assembly line-ing my Chinese homework was what made me so tempted towards the Sophomore Stupid [see Anika’s blog]. I’m so tempted to treat everything in my life as something that can be optimized—like I’m a video game character and in order to win, I have to minmax my stats. When I was little, I had always measured my success comparatively—to win at life, I had to be the best in the world at something. And to be the best, I had to pour every effort in one direction. Any type of balance meant that something was wasted. I don’t mean to disparage ambition or competitiveness. I think a healthy dose of both (though at times it has not been healthy :P) has made me who I am today. But as the classic adage that I just made up goes, “Life is like riding a unicycle. To go fast, you have to not fall off.” And in order to not fall off, you need to maintain some sort of balance. ⁠09 . As it turns out, happiness is kind of important for motivation. So I ended up dropping two classes: my history class and my topology class—and poof! 12 hours of my week (and more, since problem sets also take time outside of class) were back in my possession. Here are some things I did with those extra 12 hours the next week: I watched Your Name, a movie that LSC ⁠10 put on. I hardly ever watch movies, but I’d heard that it was a good movie, plus my friend was running it. I had a great time! It was a really sweet movie; the art style and music was fantastic. I was sobbing at the last few scenes (I’m an easy crier—I cry at most movies that are supposed to make you cry. And sometimes at movies that are not supposed to make you cry, too ⁠11 ). Instead of speedrunning my bagged lunch because I had no time, now I actually had a free hour around lunchtime! I got Vietnamese Pho with a friend at Eastern Edge, a food court on the—surprise—eastern edge of campus. After a year of promising to go to Spinjam, I went to Spinjam again! Spinjam is basically firespinning, but off fire. We gather on the lawn near East Campus ⁠12 , the Spinning Arts club provides lots of props and people to teach tricks on the props, and we spin things! I learned some cool tricks on the dragonstaff and tried to juggle it. Then the next week I had too many psets and skipped it again. ⁠13 After experiencing true freedom, I’ve forgotten why I wanted to take seven classes in the first place. I’ve realized that by trying to stuff my schedule with all the classes I could fit, I was missing out on so many other things. But then again, I’m always missing out on so many things—the FOMO at this school is real. Even after dropping two classes and taking “only” five classes, I’m still at a heavy courseload. It still feels like I’m rushing from assignment to assignment and from class to class. I wish I had more time to spend on my language classes—after every German class, I end up with ten or more new vocabulary words in my notebook and I keep meaning to turn them into flashcards, but it never happens. I wish I had more time to spend on my UROP ⁠14 . I wish I had more time to blog. I wish I had time to juggle literally and not metaphorically. But alas, such is the curse of time that we are only allowed 24 hours in a day, 7 days in a week, and 52.1429 weeks in a year. Someday, I’ll figure out how to make a time turner, so I can go back and do everything I never had the time for.

Title: Embarrassing Mistakes I Have Made…So Far
Author: Leya E. '30
Article Content: It’s been about a month since the first day of classes. Isn’t it so funny how fast time passes?. No. No it’s not. Because even though it’s only been a month, I have had SO MUCH WORK. And also this week was lowkey hell week for all the frosh since all the GIRS apparently have to have their midterms at the same time.⁠01 So it hasn’t been a good time for anyone. But you know what’s good about weeks? They end! And then it’s the weekend! Isn’t that so poetic? Anyway yes, I have had a lot of work so far, and have subsequently already been learning a lot and doing a lot of new things! Both in class, and out of it. But when you do things that you’ve never done before, you’re pretty much bound to make mistakes. But that’s ok, because mistakes are how you learn! In the wise words of Ms. Frizzle: “Take chances, make mistakes, and get messy!”⁠02 However, mistakes are often also incredibly embarrassing. So here is a list of mistakes I have made so far and how I have learned from them, ranging from slightly embarrassing to “I wanted to lock myself in my room and never come out” embarrassing. Getting to Dunkin slightly too late in the morning. My first class is at 9am on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and because I am not a morning person I often like to stop at Dunkin before class for a nice little energy drink. The only problem is that apparently everyone else has the same idea and the place is often packed. But the first few times I went I did not know to expect this, so I ended up waiting forever for my drink and subsequently either had to run to class or just leave without getting it. Lesson Learned: Order ahead like 20 minutes in advance if you want to guarantee getting your order in time. But also if you leave for an hour and come back it could still be there so don’t stress too much. Getting sniped at this angle: WHAT THE HELL CALEB The bloggers have this slack channel where we take pictures of each other around campus like little creeps.⁠03 Here is a post that can explain it much better than I can. And unfortunately on this day I was a victim of this. It was also like one of the top ten worst days of my life so. Lesson Learned: Be more aware of my surroundings i guess. Leaving a Class Early To Walk Into The Wrong Class This is the reason why the day I was sniped was the worst day of my life. On Mondays, I have a 1.5 hour lecture that starts at 9:30am. For some reason, at 10:30am I thought that the lecture started at 9 and was just going over time. This was not helped by the fact that people were just leaving the room for some reason. Usually, I check my calendar on my phone to ensure that I actually remember my schedule. For some reason, on this day my phone was dead. So I ended up leaving this lecture 30 minutes early, and then mistakenly believed that my 11am recitation started at 10:30, so I walked into the 10am recitation instead and only when I pulled out my tablet to look at my calendar did I realize my mistake. I tried to exit as nonchalantly as possible, but that was impossible because my entire backpack spilled on the floor by the doorway. I don’t actually think I learned anything from this. Waving at People Who I Actually Do Not Know I don’t consider myself to be a terribly face blind person, but I dunno when you meet a lot of new people their faces seem to all blur together. So I may or may not have made the mistake of either waving at or smiling at people who look similar to someone I have met, like, once. It is embarrassing every time it happens. Lesson Learned: Learn people’s faces…. Making a HackMIT project that doesn’t work Yeahhhh. I only figured this out after the judging was over. I was slightly suspicious beforehand but I looked at the code and realized that we had made a mistake. Oopsies! It’s okay though. We were not exactly trying to win anything, and the judges seemed to be more concerned with projects that were actual, like, business ideas anyway. If you’re curious about where we messed up, the link to the github is in my last post :3. Lesson Learned: Check to make sure your code works, and then check again, and then check a third time, and then you still probably haven’t checked enough. Being bad at throwing paper airplanes A couple weeks ago I played in an Assassin’s Guild game called Die Osingverlosung! It’s about a town in Germany that has a lottery to give land to people that they can use to farm on. It’s also about a weird stick, trains, and cake! I was the mayor, which meant my main job was to oversee contracts that people made to sell land. I also got to organize the lottery, and made the announcement at the end that I was retiring because I was, quote, “so fucking old”. I was very amused that my quote ended up making it into the wrapup packets that we got at the end of the game. I also had the goal to learn some slang(because I’m so old), and overused the phrase “no cap” a lot. However, as the mayor I was also part of a group of religious people who needed vegetables to do a ritual. In order to get the vegetables, we had to do some sort of challenge, and once someone did a challenge no one else could do it. I tried to do a challenge early, but ended up failing it, and did not go back to complete one until the only feasible challenge left was making a paper airplane. The only issue is that I have never once in my life made a paper airplane that could fly, or thrown a paper airplane correctly. Multiple minutes were spent trying to teach me how to make a paper airplane, and those minutes were all in vain. It didn’t end up mattering since we ended up getting a vegetable another way, but it was still embarrassing. Lesson Learned: Do not agree to make paper airplanes ever. And also sometimes mistakes can be both embarrassing and funny. Auditioning for a bunch of acapellas and only getting a callback for one(that I did not accept) Before classes started, all the acapellas on campus had their auditions! Creating a sight known as audition row. All the groups were lined up in one hallway with tables ready for walk-in or scheduled auditions. There are 11 acapella groups on campus,⁠04 and I ended up auditioning for 6 of them. I only got a callback for one⁠05 , and I realized that I didn’t actually want to join them, so I was 0 for 6 in audition row. It didn’t help that I also got sick the day before all the auditions started, had no water, and was also just generally nervous as hell. I think it ended up being a good thing though, because I realized that I probably wouldn’t have time for how long the rehearsals for some of the acapellas are. Lesson Learned: Sometimes you try things and they don’t work out, but at least you tried! And maybe something better will come of it :) Sitting in 6.1903 office hours waiting for a checkoff without realizing that my wifi was off and so the checkoff didn’t go through. This one is pretty self-explanatory. I did get quite frustrated waiting there, without realizing that there was a very easy solution to my problem. Oopsies. Lesson Learned: Try to exhaust all possible options for solutions before giving up. Starting all my psets the day before they’re due. Hey, so this one may or may not be a mistake that I keep making, but it’s okay because at least I know it’s a problem! The thing about psets is that they are very much not designed to be completed in one night and also usually very much not designed to be completed alone. But the problem with doing them last minute is that there’s really no time to ask other people for help and so I may or may not have yet to turn in a fully finished pset this semester. But it’s okay! Because at least I know I have a problem, and that’s the first step to solving a problem! And also it’s PNR so like at least I don’t have to worry too much about my actual grades on each pset. But um yes I would like to actually complete a pset this semester. Lesson Learned: Don’t start things the day before they’re due! Spread out your work! And don’t work alone! :3 Double booking myself and then feeling bad about having to miss something but then no one cared The aforementioned Assassin’s Guild game also happened to run at the same time as the first rehearsal for one of the acts I’m in for Next Sing, and I felt very bad about this. Ultimately, I decided to go to the game instead of the rehearsal because I also felt bad for already having to reschedule when I was going to be in the game, and I thought that maybe missing the first rehearsal wouldn’t be that bad. This line of thinking didn’t prevent me from feeling very bad about missing the rehearsal for the entire week, and thinking that something very bad was gonna happen. I then went to the second rehearsal, and nothing happened. Everything was fine. And then I felt embarrassed for worrying so much. Lesson Learned: Try not to double book yourself, but when you do at least tell someone about it. You can’t control other people’s reactions to that information, but you don’t always have to assume the worst either. Thinking that people like me less than they actually do The funny thing about this mistake is that it’s one that I’ve actually been making for years! I have this weird little tendency to think that anyone who has expressed any interest in hanging out with me only wants to do it once and that any subsequent time I see them I should make no effort to talk to them at all. And this is one mistake that I seem to never learn from. I always believe that any positive social interaction I have is some kind of fluke, and that the second I leave everyone will have completely forgotten about me. But I feel like now, somehow, I’m finally starting to learn from this mistake. I am often shocked by how many times I am waved at first. By how many times people I know excitedly come up to me to talk about something. By how many times people in a club make space for me to join their conversation. One of the most embarrassing things in the world is when you try to join a conversation, or worse, make a joke related to the conversation, and then suddenly everyone just becomes silent and stares at you. And you know what? That hasn’t happened to me here. And even if it does, I don’t really think I’ll care. I’ve found people who like hanging out with me, and it was much easier than I expected. The real embarrassing thing was how completely I was proven wrong. Lesson Learned: There is always someone out there who will like you, but you’ll never meet them if you don’t put yourself out there and believe that you can be liked. These are just some of the mistakes I’ve made so far, and I’m sure there’ll be plenty more in the future. But you know what, that just means more learning! Isn’t that so poetic?

Title: Welcome to My Museum of MIT
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: This post is inspired by this New York Times article. Like all good things, it makes me both giggle and think. The following is mostly satirical, and entirely my opinion. Some of these are MIT specific, and some are applicable to American colleges in general. tl;dr don’t read into this too strongly Apple Pencil (uncapped) Pen and paper are so 2008. Why actually write stuff down when you can fake write it down, with colors! Unfortunately, between the 6-12 hours you spend a day looking down at your iPad for notes, psets, etc., you’ve lost the most protective piece of you $100 writing utensil. Eh, screw it, you have work to do anyway and that Apple Store is far. example (note that i actually do have my cap!) Banana Hot and mushy. Cold and stringy. Somehow perfect? MIT bananas come in many varieties, but one thing ties them all together: free. Enjoy the fruits of your labor with a fruit to pair with your labor! Spot these bananas: in bulk in a random grad student’s hand; getting brown in student’s backpacks as they go from lecture to lecture; spoiling in those huge cardboard boxes in the Banana Lounge. Potassium kings, rise! 3D Printer At a tech school that supports student creation and innovation, there is naturally a strong subset of students who simply want to make things. But, due to x, y, z constraint of actually getting the things you need to make that robot/bioreactor/microscope/wall decor, the process of making isn’t what is actually hard for students. Introducing: plastic builder machine. Everyone and their mom either built their own, bought one, or goes to the Makerspace to use them. At MIT, you can make anything out of seemingly nothing. Energy Drink Welcome, youth, to late-stage capitalism! You’re beat down and exhausted, but have even more to do than when you started. But do not fear, for no matter what time of the day it is, it’s acceptable to crank out a quick 200+ mg of caffeine and get cracking on the pset. The solution to our problems is not in fixing the structures themselves, but funneling our bodies with chemicals to abide by them. Black Puffer Jacket Chic penguin? Gucci trash bag? Foreign goose? No, it’s me and my unreasonable loud, annoyingly large, brutally unwashed black puffer jacket, absolutely worked down the Infinite 7 months out of the year. +2 if you never take it off. Shaky Walker Memorial Desk Walker Memorial mostly exists in juxtapositions. So blistering hot that the TAs half-undress mid-proctor, or a Siberian cold turning my fingertips red. A cacophony of that One Large Fan™, construction outside, and everyone’s shoes, or pin-drop silence as you hear your tears fall on the page. Yet, at the end of it all, one thing remains eternal: that Shaky Walker Memorial Desk. Every corner moves as you shift your weight to erase your entire answer. The entire surface is sticky and covered in loose led. One time a spider crawled up on to my exam, and even it got so exhausted from the sight of my problem that it left.⁠01 Shaky Walker Memorial Desk is the crushing reminder that even at your darkest moments, when you’re struggling to keep yourself together, everything around you is shaking as well. Vester Matcha Black lettering on plain white wall. Black wall with a fun font of white letters. Paper cup and paper straw and paper holder with a paper napkin that disintegrate when touching your $9 latte. Minimalist cafe culture is a bore, but a necessity to be in. Sure, it’s Amazon-quality almond milk and matcha powder, but the status of walking around with the effortlessly aesthetic ~green~ is enough to pull you in. Men’s 3-in-1 Body Wash MIT teaches you to examine every edge case of a system–to consider every possible “technicality”. And when you’re busy analyzing every possibility of x, y, z thing, you might get so swept away that you forget other, more important daily activities. Sure! It is technically soap. Not in a way that works according to anyone’s standard, but just technically enough for you to say you showered with “soap”! -10 if you’re a course 6 and hurting the reputation. Dome Photo Maybe parts of MIT are not totally idyllic…except one. LinkedIn picture, Instagram story, graduation picture. All of them in front of that big ass dome. And honestly, they should be! For all you’ve done, flaunt that dome as much as you want. Starchy White T-Shirt MIT has an endowment that allows for ~$2.32 million per student. And, while that endowment goes to many, many things for students, one of those is not towards t-shirt design. MIT will force dozens of free t-shirts on you, and together combined they could make 3 ± 2 quality shirts. On their own, though, they are some combination of black/white/red lettering with few enough threads to scratch my back every time I take it off. Jet Tag Statistically, you’re not course 16.⁠02 Still, if you’ve had absolutely any association with BlueOrigin, SpaceX, or the like, you will have these fabric bands hanging from every surface on your backpack. Two Big Guys Touching on One Electric Scooter It could be the middle of the night, riding across the Charles with the wind in your hair after a night out. It could 10:58 AM, rushing to your next class down the Outfinite. No matter what time or where you are, their love is eternal. A modern Brokeback Mountain. Two frat guy student-athletes full-body touching as they share one electric scooter. Niche Instant Ramen A college classic. In a rush and can’t eat dinner? Want a late-night snack? Go for the classic: instant ramen. But nay nay, this is no Maruchan, for we have an H-Mart next to campus, so we dine on the exquisite, niche ramens. .75 cents/package?? Ha! These fine-dining courses can go upwards of $6. Buldak, you are our nation’s ramen. Green Couch, Blue Wall MIT is known for its brutalist architecture: harsh, square concrete buildings spread out across equally grey sidewalks. Despite all this, MIT makes up for its bland outsides with equal and opposite insides for its living communities. I wake up, and I see green couches and blue walls. I go to sleep after escaping from my green couches and blue walls. I am nothing without my gaudy neon interior decor that I call home. TeaDo Boba You’re in college, you’re likely poor, and definitely a sugar addict. Fortunately, you and everyone else has one (1) accessible option that is seemingly always open and always present, whether you want it or not. VC event? TeaDo Boba. Study break? TeaDo boba. Club meeting? TeaDo boba. Grapefruit, mango, strawberry, popping, pearls, big fat colorful straw, onigiri, and those damn plastic cups everywhere. What are you getting everyday? TeaDo boba. Quant Merch One of the most accurate stereotypes about MIT is that finance recruiters are hunting you down to get absolutely any of your potential math genius to make money for other people. Whether or not you buy into this doesn’t matter, for we allllll attend those super fancy free dinners with Jane Street, if not just for the free meal and open bar. And at the end of the night, the best gift is not that of a referral or even a job, but that iconic HRT shirt that you will wear until the end of time. You make 6 figures, but free clothes look better anyway. Rubik’s Cube Canonically, I know multiple people who Cube™ (v.) when they are stressed. In vibes and assumption, many MIT students learned how to solve a Rubik’s Cube as their first algorithm. In perpetuity, students will walk around and flick their fingers until all the colors line up in the cute but also necessary-for-my-autism sort of way. Psychotropic Medication The kids are not alright. Maybe this is because we talk more openly about these things, which is good. Maybe this is because we have much easier access to psychiatrists, which is good. Maybe this is because, over time, the intensity of college has grown from a personality-forming to a personality-sucking experience. Nonetheless, the kids are aware of their issues, and trying to work through them. Free Listening Guy He comes and he goes, but he is always on the steps of Lobby 7 when you need him. He holds a big, white, simplistic sign only telling people that he will listen for free. Most of the time people just walk on by, but sometimes they’ll stop. At a place where this is so much so say and no culture to talk about it, it takes a random man offering his time for us to open up, light-heartedly or toward our true souls, for the realest conversations to happen. Chalkboards High school is for those juvenile whiteboards, stuffed with that squeaky, smelly Expo Marker. The big dogs, though? We play with chalk. The dust gets everywhere, it’s impossible to read from afar, it makes awful noises, and it snaps in half at the most important moments. But who cares? This is academia, we have math to do, baby. MassTech Pants Y2K fashion is back and bigger than ever. And while most MIT students wouldn’t dare to flaunt the insanely low-rise jeans, belly button piercing, or hair tinsel to class, there’s a certain Couture that never goes out of style. Booty shorts, tank tops, and, of course, the sweatpants, are the proudest items of merch that most MIT students own. The Coop is for the grandparents, MassTech is for the youth. Taken from their instagram @wearemasstech Box Hair Dye College is for experimenting, right? You don’t want your parents to know that suddenly you’re an alternative emo punk singer, but you also definitely want to be. Let the fleeting permanence of your existence college take over with impermanent box hair dye! Do it in the bathroom at 4 AM before a midterm, or have your friends do it in the EC courtyard during REX. It might be one of the last times you can do orange and purples streaks across your hair before an employer judges you, so why not? Brass Rat It’s been a long road, and you’ve experienced all of the above. Things are starting to get serious now…you’re two years into the relationship, you’re feeling pretty good about not leaving, and you think it’s time to tie the knot? And just like that, a fall proposal (Ring Premiere) and a spring wedding (Ring Delivery)! Like all marriages, it comes with its ups and downs. But you’ll both be there, through thick and thin!

Title: experiments on a sample size of one
Author: Ellie F. '28
Article Content: I spend a lot of showers and walks and lectures thinking about how I make friends and why I use my phone so much and what makes me phase out during class. Then I proceed to not change anything about my life. And I wasted an hour of lecture. Does this sound familiar? I think that since coming to college, nearly every facet of my life has improved considerably. I can’t tell how much that was driven by me, internally, and how much of it was my new environment, a result of being repotted when I was rootbound for so long. Either way, I picked up bad habits in freshman year that I still haven’t managed to shed, through a mix of complacency or inertia or some helpless sense of it is what it is. Now, I’m starting the second half of my life at MIT, and something (someone? someplace?) has lifted the mist out of my brain. I’ve hypothesized so long about what changes I’d make to my life if I could. Somewhere in there, I forgot that I just—can. I have will, and willpower, and I do hard things all the damn time. I’ve started carrying out what I call experiments, in a loving bastardization of the scientific method I learned in 5th Grade General Science. It was also that year, I think, when I read 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (only it was a version for teenagers). I don’t remember much from that book–I learned what marijuana was (and that I shouldn’t use it), the definition of conscience (I pronounced it con-SCI-ence in my head for years), and the concept of “roping up”. I’m realizing now that, after years of playing telephone with my past self, this idea has probably warped in my mind from what it originally meant, but this is how I think about it: when setting goals for yourself, you should involve as many people as possible. If you can’t get anyone else to join you, just broadcast it to your friends. Be motivated from their support, or at least from not wanting to disappoint them. That’s what this blog is–a declaration of intent to whoever my audience is (hi) and something to hold me accountable. I hope it’s also entertaining. Phoneless Friday It’s Phoneless Friday! Are you celebrating? And I don’t want to hear some lame excuse like “it’s not Friday”–Phoneless Friday is a state of mind. I’m pretty sure there are very few people that are happy with their relationship with their phone. My years-deep rut tends to go like this: slide her out of my pocket, unlock, open Discord by instinct, no new messages because I did this a minute ago. And if I scroll over to Instagram may god help us all. The solution is far too obvious, right? Like, if you want to use your phone less, you can just not have your phone. Except, for some reason, this is not something I ever considered as a real possibility, and it seems to ring similarly for everyone I talk to about it. But, for me, a phone is essentially my MIT ID, credit card, how I communicate with people, and a camera. The rest I really don’t want to think about. The first two functions are trivially replaceable with their physical counterparts, and I can check my messages whenever I open my computer. I haven’t figured out a substitute for the camera yet, but I might buy one in the future. Anyways, I’m now unceremoniously stuffing my phone in the back of my shelf for at least a day a week. It’s working surprisingly well–I thought I’d be missing her like an earworm in my dopamine receptors, but it’s mostly silence. And it’s spilled over into phoneful days too. I’ve been capitalizing on this by starting a competition with two of my friends with regards to screen time, and I do not plan to lose. Getting a good grade in going to lecture I have been a chronic lecture skipper since my second illness in freshman year. On my calendar, I would gray out the classes I didn’t go to, and it was looking like Boston winter out there. My justification for this, and I do think this is a valid reason, is that I just don’t learn well in lecture. My brain wants problems to chew on, and in lecture, it dreamwalks straight into hopelessly lost just a scant ten minutes in. So, in my four semesters here, my taste of lecture has mostly been reading the lecture notes days later, scrambling to find a foothold for that week’s pset. I really didn’t think that would work this time around, with more units than ever, and I really didn’t care to find out, either. Enter this experiment: going to every lecture and recitation I can (still scheduled some overlaps… old habits die hard), sitting near the front, and actually answering questions. I don’t take notes. If I have my computer open in any capacity, my tabs will converge to crosswithfriends or the gnome game. And on my iPad, I use Procreate to do all my work. From experience, let me assure you that trying to take notes in an app meant for digital art results in some really great doodles and not many notes at all. Now, going to lecture has started feeling like the professors are teaching straight to me. And I actually understand the algorithms we go over in class! Maybe I’ll use my tuition for something after all. Microdosing Hiking I work out every day now! And my chronic back pain is actually meaningfully getting better! This is not about that. This is about how I don’t have a car or the time to go hiking. When you think about it, hiking has two components. The first one is going up, and the second one is being in nature. You can’t argue with me because I’m the one writing this blog post, and also because I’m right. Anyway, if I can’t really hike I may as well get as close as I can. Going up is easy. As it happens, I live on the eighth floor, and the law has had the foresight to mandate a staircase in every building with more than one floor for me, specifically. So, whenever I’m alone (I am not going to make anyone else do this with me) and not in physical discomfort, I climb all eight floors up to my room. The nature part is trickier. I’ve been looking out the windows as I climb. There are trees there. Open House Making friends is so hard. I want to walk up to someone, mutually lay bare the most interesting dimensions of ourselves, and agree to meet up once a week ad infinitum. Maybe for boba. Instead, we have started asking about each other’s majors. Something has gone very wrong. I haven’t figured out how to completely break out of the conversational flowchart that ends in following someone’s Instagram and never messaging them ever. Please email me at ellieee@mit.edu if you’ve made progress on this. But a related, and maybe easier, problem is on how to maintain friendships with people you already like. Because if I reached out to and played Calendar Tetris against and spent meaningful time with everyone I’d like to see on a weekly basis, they’d be performing an autopsy on me. However, I am not dead! And I’ve maybe developed a way of reaching out to people once and seeing them semi-regularly regardless. AND it doesn’t involve joining any clubs at all! That might be a new one for me. My roommate and I call it Open House, and it’s two hours of Please Come By and Hang Out (If You Can) each Friday. On Google Calendar, it takes the form of a recurring event with a long invitees list. In my room, it’s bread ends from Flour, juice, and a different subset of cool people every week. I’m afraid attendance might fizzle out with the onslaught of everything (I am gesturing extremely broadly), but the beauty of Open House is that it’s just as good with one person as with ten.

Title: i have slept 30 hours in the past two days
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: on thursday i assembled foamboard posters for esp cascade for two hours, then went to puzzle club at 5:30, and then after that i started baking a cake. as i baked the cake my throat started feeling more and more sore. oh no i thought oh no aaaaaaaaa frick PLEASE NO. i drank some milk but that did not fix my throat being sore. i went to steve⁠01 study break in walounge,⁠02 where my throat felt even more sore. at 10:52 i ask the tetazoo group chat if anyone has nyquil or any other pain reliever; tori gives me some advil. at 11:28 scarlet tells me to sleep. at a little bit past twelve, i play the daily catfishing. at 12:15 i finally turn the lights off and go to sleep at 10:30 my first alarm goes off. this is because my first class on monday wednesday friday is 5.112⁠03 which has lecture at 11. my throat is still sore. it hurts to swallow. i decide that i don’t want to go to class. i ask sean to ask around for cough drops; he gives me two handfuls from an. i set another alarm for 1pm and go back to sleep. at 1pm my second alarm goes off. coincidentally, 1pm is when my second class of the day is: 18.03.⁠04 i decide i don’t want to go to class. but before i sleep this time i stumble through typing out an email to my terrascope advisor telling her that i am sick and will be missing class. i set another alarm for 4pm and go back to sleep. at 4pm my third alarm goes off. by this time i have missed all three classes for the day. i laze around in bed for a bit. eventually i decide that drinking water and eating food are good for me, so i get out of bed for the first time. if you check the clock i have now slept for almost 16 hours. that’s a lot of hours! i drag myself to tetazoo kitchen on the other end of hall, where i microwave myself some rice and spam. i sit in glounge⁠05 and watch people play tomodachi life. tetazoo has played tomodachi life almost continuously for the past few days. it is bad. there is tomodachi life happening at least until 6am. i finally make my own mii! yay! i remember i have a quiz to do for 12.004⁠06 and go to my room and speedrun it. i eat another bowl of rice and spam. eventually as i go into the kitchen hua tells me to go to sleep. i say “but… tomodachi life….” she says “don’t ‘tomodachi life’ me”. fine. i go back to my room. sean asks if i am going to putz tetazoo mixer. i decide i don’t want to go to that, nor the fifth west fallout-themed party after that. i set a timer on my phone for 12:00, because sean’s birthday pancakes are tonight, and go to sleep. it is 7:30pm. at 11:49pm i wake up spontaneously. at 12:02 sean wakes up because rory is calling him because it is his birthday pancakes. i decide that i don’t want to go to birthday pancakes and just lay in bed. i play the daily catfishing. twenty minutes later, sean and his partner come back. i say happy birthday again. i go to sleep. it is 12:30am. at 4:21am my friend will texts me to say he is in tetazoo. i do not respond because i am asleep. at 11:30am my alarm goes off. i turn it off and set another timer for 2:30pm, but then decide to just wake up. i am feeling a lot better! it doesn’t hurt to swallow anymore. i read a friend’s blog post. i eat a tangerine. i shower. i eat another tangerine, maybe. i go to the kitchen and toast a bagel and eat it with cream cheese. i refill my water bottle. i talk to sage and jesse and charlie. i eat some broccoli. i toast another bagel and eat it with cream cheese. i look at my spanish reading. i go back to my room. i lay in bed. what do i have to do? spanish class is the most urgent. i read funes el memorioso, then i decide i would rather listen to it audiobook style. i play some chess. i read funes el memorioso in english. i text some friends. i read about and watch an interview with argentinian neuroscientist rodrigo quian quiroga. i decide to skip dance troupe rehearsal. my alarm goes off. i decide to write this blog post. maybe i will finally get chipotle? thank goodness i got sick on friday, i think. thank goodness i didn’t get sick on thursday, when i had a chem quiz, or on wednesday, when i had a diffeq midterm. thank goodness i didn’t get sick on days where i actually couldn’t miss class. thank goodness i did not have super urgent work to do. thank goodness i can fade off the face of the earth for 30 hours and my life goes on.

Title: trying to find poetry under calculus
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content: It’s October–which means it’s been almost two years since my first visit to MIT. I visited MIT the first time in October 2024 and loved it, which is part of the reason I chose to be here today. And one of my strongest first memories of this place—the one that cemented the nerdy MIT culture in my mind–was the MIT Museum. It was different from any other museum I’ve seen. I found almost every exhibit interesting (which is not typical of me in normal museums, where I lose interest and breeze past the exhibits). They had an exhibit on the dangers of AI (pretty relevant today tbh), a whole section dedicated to the inventions made from MIT (one that stood out to me the most was a keyboard algorithm that tracked people’s finger movements to detect Parkinson’s disease), a pink chicken, a taxidermied ‘mermaid’ in a glass case (…which was quite frightening), a juggling machine, and a bunch of other cool things! the pink chicken holograms! we're truly living in the future terrifying... I was actually so inspired by this exhibit, that the first thing I did when I got home was to order a unicycle on Amazon (it took me a month to learn after that, but now I can ride one!) Previous Next If you like STEM and/or weird things, I highly encourage you to visit–to this day, I still go to the MIT Museum area (there’s a great cafe next to it!) to do my problem sets and so I can somehow absorb the ingenuity emanating off of the exhibits inside. But my favorite thing I saw was an exhibit that let you write poems to the next person that sees the exhibit with random (but somewhat above average in nerdiness/mit-esqueness) words. When I got there, the message that the previous person left me was this: trying to find poetry under calculus. I LOVE CALCULUS!! AND POETRY WITH CALCULUS!! Calculus was very definitely my favorite class in high school, not only because it was the first math class that felt like it wasn’t just memorizing formulas, but also because I loved my teacher (shoutout Ms. Kalbag–most goated high school teacher I’ve had, tbh) and classmates. Our class was small, with 12ish people, so we were especially close-knit for a class in a public high school, and many shenanigans were pulled. I have so many stories from that class. ⁠01 One thing we started was the tradition of trying to make our teacher laugh when grading our exams by writing math-related jokes in the margins of our tests. Usually it was cheesy jokes like “I see you have graph paper…you must be plotting something evil with those weapons of math instruction!”. At this time, I was also a fan of reading David Morin’s physics textbooks. I highly recommend them–David Morin is the GOAT of physics textbooks (I think he still teaches at Harvard, so maybe I can have the chance to meet him someday and get his autograph :O). Not only is his writing style super clear and engaging, but his textbooks also have limericks in them! Some limerick samples–the first one is from Special Relativity for the Enthusiastic Beginner, and the second one is from Introductory Classical Mechanics, both by David Morin. I was so inspired by these demonstrations-by-limerick and I thought it would be cool if I could write a proof on my calculus final exam in poem form. Our teacher had told us that we needed to know how to prove the quotient rule, so that was a natural choice of proof. As a reminder, the quotient rule says that if we have a function that can be written as the quotient of two other functions, the derivative of that function looks like this: I always forget which way the negative sign goes… But what format of poem would I use? God forbid trying to prove it in 17 syllables, so haiku was off the table. A limerick was still too short to cram the proof into. Aha–a Shakespearean Sonnet! I’d never read actually read Shakespeare beyond acting in a small school production of A Midsummer’s Night’s Dream in sixth grade (and it was very much a shortened version, but still a decent length for my sixth grade self’s memory), but “Shakespeare” was the most unrelated thing to calculus I could think of, and so writing a proof in Shakespearean Sonnet form would maximize hilarity. But first, I needed to find out what a Shakespearean sonnet was. A quick Google search gave me the structure: iambic pentameter in an abab cdcd efef gg rhyme scheme. …Okayyyy, I still didn’t know what an “iambic pentameter” is. Another Google search showed me that it’s a type of rhythm that goes “da DUM da DUM da DUM da DUM da DUM” (one ‘da DUM’ makes an iamb, and five of them make pentameter!). Here, a “da” is an unstressed syllable and a “DUM” is a stressed syllable. Here’s an excerpt of Shakespeare’s Sonnet 12, which has iambic pentameter, as a demonstration: When I do count the clock that tells the time (hmm that seems a bit redundant, but who am I to judge Shakespeare? Maybe in his time, the clocks could tell the temperature too.) The bolded syllables are the stressed syllables. If you say it out loud, it sounds very nice and rhythmic, like a heartbeat! After culturing myself on Shakespeare, I sat down to write. I knew I wanted the last couplet (the two lines that have the gg rhyme scheme) to conclude my proof with some kind of Q.E.D. (a mathematician’s “ta-da, i did it!”. it stands for some fancy latin thing), so I started with that. It was hard figuring out the iambic pentameter—it took a couple minutes per line of me repeating it very slowly, putting stress in different places, and trying to hear if that sounded natural. I still don’t know how people write meter in poetry. The three quatrains (stanzas with four lines each) were even trickier to get right. I spent three hours fiddling with my lines, juggling the rhyme scheme, iambic pentameter, and of course, making sure it was mathematically valid. Midway through my composing, I realized that my initial variable choice of the familiar x and y could not work with the rhyme scheme—too few words rhymed with ‘x’: X, although not complex, did more than perplex: the rhyme objects! Sorry. Although it saddened me to have to rework a full two quatrains, I knew I had to make the sacrifice. In order to use poetry to do calculus, I had to use calculus to do poetry: I applied the familiar technique of changing the variables (you might call it u-substitution). Instead of x, I switched to rho, and lo! It worked. (Eventually). Then came another hour of constantly tabbing over to RhymeZone, whispering lines to myself, and digitally thumbing through the thesaurus…and ta-da, I did it! (or should I say, Q.E.D.?) Here’s the final product, as written on the back of my final (sadly, our teacher lied and there was no ‘prove the quotient rule’ question, so I was never able to see how my proof held up, points-wise): To prove the quotient rule, we use the chain Apply the product, then we simplify To do that, do some math, and use your brain For now, We have a function f of y. With that, We first let equal u o’er rho The prime of that, with product, now shall be D u d y times rho inverse, and lo Add u d one oe’r rho d y, you see. For one o’er rho, do chain rule (almost there!) And you’ll get this (unless you are a fool) The minus prime of rho o’er rho that’s square Combine, replace, and lo, the quotient rule! So now we’ve proved it’s true, as you can see And thus it’s proven, and therefore, Q E D. In regular form, the proof looks like this: So there you go! The quotient rule, proved in Shakespearean Sonnet form. Looking back, it was actually a very fun three hours–and I’m surprised it only took me three hours. I’ve realized that I’m a big fan of these constrained writing challenges. ⁠02 Perhaps next time I’ll write something in pilish ⁠03 for Pi Day, or in a post without the letter e ⁠04 for e day (that’s February seventy-first). ⁠05

Title: My Unusually Long Prequel to Sophomore Year
Author: Lauren W. '29
Article Content: Happy FDOC and FWOC! Realistically, this is going up a couple weeks after FWOC, but at the time I am starting to write this, it is the first day of classes! As a fall athlete and sorority member, my time at MIT before FDOC is a lot longer and busier than most students, so come with me as I tell you about pre-season and sorority recruitment! I’m on the MIT varsity women’s soccer team, and our move in day was on August 18 this year. Since our first official game was on September 1, over a week before classes started, we have to move in a couple weeks early to prepare for season. It was so exciting to reunite with everyone on the team after being separated all summer long, and of course meet our new frosh! Last year’s pre-season, when we were scrimmaging D1 Harvard within the first week of practice. We started off with two-a-days⁠01 and scrimmages for a couple weeks before our first official game. We would normally have a lighter morning session, and then a harder afternoon practice or scrimmage within our own team or against another school. In between practices, I would hang out with others on the team. We would get coffee, play Fortnite (mobile), take naps, and do literally everything together. It was so much fun. In the evenings, we would plan mixers for our frosh with other sports on campus. This early in the year, there are only other fall sports on campus with us: women’s volleyball, field hockey, football, men’s soccer, and men’s waterpolo. Last year as a freshman, these mixers were super exciting as I was meeting a bunch of new people and future friends at every one. This year was still fun, and I was happy to reunite with my friends on other fall sports teams. The current sophomore women’s soccer class going out to dinner in Boston together! On the first day we didn’t have afternoon practice, each grade on the team decided to do its own class bonding in the evening. It wasn’t something anyone planned as a team, we each just did it on our own. I thought it was so cute that our first instinct on a semi-off day was to spend quality time with each other. I absolutely love my team and it really feels like a second family. Our second scrimmage against SNHU, came out with the dub! We then drove all the way to New Hampshire (a whopping 1 hour to drive to an entirely different state)⁠02 , to play SNHU in our last scrimmage before the season started. I started my first game at MIT in this one, but unfortunately got into a bad tackle and sprained my left ankle. I haven’t had many significant injuries in my time playing soccer, so I’m not used to sitting out, and it’s been pretty hard. Walking out to our first official game of the season at our lovely home field, Roberts! I still was not able to play in this game a week later. It’s hard because my ankle has healed a lot but it hurts to sprint, change direction, and kick, all things absolutely necessary to actually play soccer. But, I have had a great time watching my teammates do awesome things on the field, and it has been nice to let my body rest. I know that when I’m able to come back, I’ll have even more motivation to play at my best. Since then, I’ve been taking a back seat on soccer, which meant I could focus more on rush! I am in a sorority, Kappa Alpha Theta (Theta for short), and we have FSR, Fully Structured Recruitment, the weekend before school starts. If you want to learn more about the details of FSR and Panhel, there is another amazing blog that goes more into it here. Now that I’m a sophomore, I got to experience the other side of rush for the first time, actually recruiting freshmen to Theta. I honestly was not the most involved in my sorority last year, but recruitment was still super fun and I feel a lot more connected to Theta and the amazing people in it. Me and some of my famline! My grandbig, big, and one of my aunts! My famline is one of my favorite parts of being in Theta. Every year after rush, new members go on kitesises or sister dates, which are basically hangouts with different people in the chapter. Then, around mid October, they rank and get matched with a member one year older than them to be their big. Last October, I got matched with my amazing big, Selin. My grandbig, Joanne, is Selin’s big, and my great grandbig was Joanne’s big. This chain of bigs is how famlines are formed, and it’s amazing to have a close group of people in different grades to look up to. My famline is pretty big because my grandbig now has three littles, so I have two aunts who also add to the famline. It was fun reuniting with my famline during when everyone came back to prepare for rush. It also was super exciting to talk to PNMs⁠03 ! The freshmen were so cute and it is crazy to think I was in their exact spot only one year ago. Preference Round⁠04 and Bid Night⁠05 are both on the same day, and then the next day is FDOC, so it is a very fast turnaround. The women’s soccer team normally can’t make Bid Night because we always have a game that evening, but we do our own little bid night after our game and all hang out at the Theta house and order food. I love our new class so much, and I’m super excited to go on many kitesises this fall and meet them! My twin star famline on FDOC morning! Theta has twin star famlines, which are temporary famlines to welcome the new members into the sorority. Everyone in my twin star famline is on the soccer team, so we are all super close already. It’s my first time being a big in this situation, and I love my cute twin star little⁠06 . It’s also a Panhel tradition to wear our Bid Night shirts all of FDOC and take pictures on Killian before classes start. It is really nice, especially as a freshman, because you can instantly spot new friends and people to sit with in class when you’re wearing the same shirt! Last year’s FDOC, when all the sororities congregated for pictures on Killian The past couple weeks have been amazing, and although classes starting isn’t my favorite thing, I know this semester is going to be super fun. I’m excited for soccer season and to come back from injury and compete for the NEWMAC and of course THE NATTY, I’m excited to get an amazing little and add to my awesome fam, I’m excited to be back with all of my friends, and I’m excited for everything this semester will bring that I can’t predict yet. If you can’t tell, I’m really looking forward to this fall, and I can’t wait to bring you guys along with me this time!

Title: Roadtrip Roadtrip
Author: Richard O. '28
Article Content: I think one of the best parts about being in college is having the freedom to virtually do whatever you want, including taking a 12-hour drive to the neighboring country upstairs on a random weekend for the fun of it. It’s even better when you get convinced by some of your friends to go with only a few messages in a group chat. Previous Next So yea. We got a rental car, left campus, and drove to Canada. At 1 PM on a Friday afternoon. And to be honest…it was definitely worth it. Canada is honestly really beautiful, as I hope the photos below will depict. Beautiful skies in upstate New York as we avoided the New England Storm Powerlines seem to be the trees of upstate NY and Canada SPENCER! JAELYNN! Previous Next After a Cane’s stop, a Walmart stop for an SD card for my camera, a gas station stop across from a farm that smelled a lot like a farm, and a Burger King stop, we finally made it across the border at like midnight. From there, we spent the night at one of my relatives’ places in Toronto and planned to set off for Niagara Falls the next morning. Don't remember what this city was called but some of the architects in Canada seem to take inspo from futuristic city movies. (Or maybe it's the other way around) More powerlines And towers. And streetlights. Previous Next After about a 90-minute drive that was turned into 2 hours thanks to Siri rerouting us on a path that supposedly had “less traffic”, which doesn’t really work when most people on the highway are probably also using that same detour… we finally made it to Niagara Falls. My family actually came to visit in 2012 to see my relatives when I was like 7 or something, but we only saw it from the US side, and I can now say that seeing it from the Canadian side is definitely so much better. But you can only experience so much from the top. So of course, the three of us decided to get a boat ticket to get up close and personal, which helped me get some fun photos. Previous Next Oh…and for whatever reason, the entire area surrounding the falls has been transformed into an insane tourist town that seemed to be centered on circus-like entertainment and all-you-can-eat food stations, which was quite the stark difference from the peaceful falls down the road. Previous Next Anyways, after Niagara we decided we wanted to touch some grass so we found this park with a beatiful hiking trail not too far from the falls and did some exploring. Previous Next We probably spent like an hour and half at the park, before heading back to Toronto in the afternoon to tour the city. Previous Next Maybe its just me but…I kinda like Toronto a little more than Boston… Previous Next We ended the day getting some Thai food in the city before taking the subway back and preparing to drive home that upcoming Sunday morning. While debating what time we would reasonably wake up, we started considering potential detours we could make on our way back to see some other cool places that we could pass by. Eventually, after lots of discussions trying to convince me that a detour wouldn’t result in us getting back to campus at like 2AM, we made a stop at Watkins Glen in New York…and honestly it was so worth the extra time. Genuinely such a beautiful place, and I think some of the photos below will be some of my favorite photos ever. Previous Next We were basically like Lewis and Clark. Previous Next So yeah, that was our Canada trip in a nutshell. All this to say that if, on a random summer day, one of your friends from freshman year calculus says they want to take a road trip somewhere up north, you should say yes. Because there are a lot of beautiful things out there to see.

Title: i went camping again
Author: Victor D. '27
Article Content: Last weekend, I went camping with my living group (Putz in East Campus) in Myles Standish State Forest, Southern Massachusetts. We went camping in early October last year, which was far too cold, overcast, and rainy. Moving our trip was definitely the right decision; warm enough even to take a swim in the pond! would you consider this a meadow? when they told us we were going to a meadow this isn't what i imagined... this is where we went swimming. i mean i didn't because i don't like the feeling of being wet outside of the water lol Previous Next Unfortunately, the area we went to didn’t have much elevation compared to last year when we submitted Monte Monadnock in New Hampshire. But our walk around the pond was nice. My friend and I were reminded of our walk around Walden Pond we did last semester, so we picked up our conversation on panpsychism from back then. For what it’s worth, you may appreciate having talked about the transcendentalists in your high school English classes because I just can’t stop thinking about them whenever I’m near a small body of water anywhere in New England. It’s always nice to get away from MIT and to have a day or two to be free of problem sets and “the grind”. Though come backing is always a struggle, and I’ve just barely caught up with my classes even though it’s been a week since camping. I think I’ll miss these activities with my living group. This is my last time I’ll go on this camping trips with them, and I’ll miss the conversations that come up when we immerse ourselves in the forest.

Title: a love letter to McCormick
Author: Hala K. '29
Article Content: As I think about coming back for this school year,⁠01 I can’t help but realize that my daily routine will look a little different. When I step out of the Great Dome after classes, I’ll walk straight toward the Student Center instead of taking my usual left toward Maseeh. My amazon packages and doordash deliveries will need to be addressed to Vassar Street rather than Memorial Drive. Visiting most of my closest friends will no longer mean simply taking an elevator down a few floors but instead walking across Briggs field. And every time I walk down dorm row, I’ll have to walk past my favorite building on campus – with renovation signs staring back at me. For the next 2 years, McCormick Hall – MIT’s only all-female residence – will be closing for renovation… and I’m devastated. It’s hard to put all of my thoughts in a single blog but this is an attempt at it: some context on McCormick: It’d be crazy to write a blog about McCormick without a quick history lesson. All of the information here is sourced from McCormick’s history page – extra shoutout to the amazing essay by alumni Tara Venkatadri included in this page. McCormick was started by Katharine McCormick in an effort to show that women belong in scientific fields and by extension, at MIT. In 1963, McCormick’s west tower⁠02 opened. By the next year, the number of female applicants to MIT had doubled.
